Side lying bottle feeding offers several advantages, particularly in terms of positioning and mimicking the natural breastfeeding experience. This method allows baby to be in a more relaxed and comfortable position, which can reduce the risk of choking and overfeeding as gravity aids in the natural flow of milk. The side-lying position also closely resembles the way a baby nurses at the breast, promoting a familiar experience for baby. 

Using your breastfeeding pillow is a great way to support baby in this position. The pillow provides stability through baby’s trunk while allowing your arm to rest without tension. The other advantage of feeding in this position is the ability to pump at the same time. There are many families who are in the middle of triple feeding, which is very time consuming. By bottle feeding in side lying at the breast (but not in the breast), the ability to pull at the same time is still there, streamlining the overall timing of the feeding. This picture shows how to have baby in a side lying bottle feeding position on the breastfeeding pillow while still having room for the pump flanges and pumping. It should be taking around 15 minutes to bottle feed baby, and most pumping sessions are between 15-20 minutes.

Parallel pumping is a technique coined by Kathleen McCue of @metropolitanbreastfeeding. It involves using a breastpump to pump one breast while simultaneously nursing baby on the other. Kathleen recommends using a pumping bra to hold the pump in place, then latching baby to the other breast. ⁣
⁣
If you are currently caught in the arduous cycle of triple feeding (nursing, then double pumping, then supplementing baby with your pumped milk) to increase supply, you may find the parallel pumping technique much more manageable. Instead of triple feeding, you would parallel pump at every feeding and then supplement with your pumped milk, if necessary. ⁣
⁣
Parallel pumping can also be done when you need to create a stash for your return to work or school. You can do this a few times a day, or only when you happen to need some extra milk. Have you tried parallel pumping? ⁣

So what is “Triple Feeding”??

This means you are feeding baby at the breast, then supplementing followed by pumping to protect your supply. You are feeding three ways in a sense. This is not meant to be a forever thing. It is honestly not sustainable physically or mentally.

Triple feeding can be beneficial for a short period of time but it is important to figure out WHY you are needing to triple feed in the first place. 

Are you having low supply? Is baby not transferring enough? There is a reason for this! It is important to work with a LC to figure out what exactly is going on. Remember, I like to call  us LC’s detectives!

Triple feeding is a TEMPORARY plan lactation consultants will put patients on to help them reach their infant feeding goals. It may be used when there is low supply or baby is not latching well. It involves three parts to feeding:
1. Latching baby, often for a set amount of time
2. Supplementing the baby, by bottle, tube at the breast, cup or syringe
3. Pumping to increase or maintain supply

This plan is EXHAUSTING because congratulations you now have unexpected twins: you’re feeding the baby and your pump which doubles the amount of work you’re doing. This should really be done under the care of an IBCLC with an exit plan or directions for how to pivot. If you were given this plan in the hospital, but no follow up appointment was set or detailed plan for how and when to shift, that was unfair. For some, doing this too long can create a massive oversupply, which has its own issues. For others, this will leave them deflated and abandoning breastfeeding before they were ready. 

If you’re on a triple feeding plan, why? Is it truly from the maternal side because of low supply? Find the root. Is it from a medication or thyroid issue or a blood loss from birth? Targeting those should see an increase in supply and a decrease in the need to pump and supplement. Is it from a poorly feeding baby? Have ties been assessed and addressed? Is baby a preemie but nearing full term? If a baby is not feeding well from the breast and there is plenty of milk, this is not a parent issue but a baby issue that needs appropriately managed. In my experience it’s almost always a tongue tie driving the struggle and a multidisciplinary team (pediatric dentist/ENT, occupational/physical/speech therapist, chiropractor and/or craniosacral therapist) are needed to help get baby back on track.

Triple feeding...is...so...hard...

While some moms never have to worry about it, the recommendation to triple feed is very common, especially in the first few days of baby's life.

What does triple feeding do? It increases the amount demanded and triggers to your brain to start producing more milk.

If you continue to demand more and more, yet your body is not producing more and more after 5ish days, I want to know WHY.

IMO, all moms who are triple feeding should be under the care of a lactation professional + a pediatric provider. If supply does increase or milk "comes in", have a weaning plan in place. If milk supply doesn't increase to meet baby's demands, I want to know WHY.

The most important thing is that your baby is fed and gaining weight. The worst thing would be that baby keeps losing weight or is not getting enough calories to support important daily activities like eating and short wake windows.

I want your newborn to be a bit feisty - I always pause when a parent tells me their newborn is "chill".

I love breastfeeding.

I remember a friend of mine asking if it hurt with Finn. “Oh no not at all!” 

And then came Liva. Our journey wasn’t easy, we started off in the NICU and every time she tried she only got 2-3 ml. Until I started using a shield and she took off. 

But then we started to deal with supply issues as a baby on a shield is not latched on. No one told me I still should be pumping in addition to using the shield.

So we tried to ditch the shield. And then.. it HURT. Cracked and bleeding and scabbed nipples. We were often both in tears.

I breastfed Finn til 2.5 and it was easy and beautiful. I told Tim this time: now I know why moms decide not to try anymore. 

Still, I was determined. Maybe a bit too much even, I could have gone easier on myself. But knowing what was up ahead and how beautiful this journey can be, I wasn’t ready to let go. 

Thanks to Dr. Newman’s clinic in Toronto we found out she had a posterior tongue tie and a minor lip tie. 

They also gave me Domperidone to increase my flow and supply, I never had supply issues but if the flow isn’t fast enough for the baby, they can’t empty your breast and then you start dealing with supply issues. So we increased the flow, got her tongue and lip tie lasered and even though her latch is still painful at times, we have a totally different baby.

From not being able to be put down or being held by anyone other than me, to happily going to others or having some floor time by herself.

From hour feeds to 15 minutes, from up all night to sleeping 6-8 hour stretches. 

And so, I get to enjoy the beauty again, the 3-4 months of struggles are now replaced by breastfeeding bliss. 

Fed is best, always. And I understand now from my own experience how hard it is. The worries about your baby not growing, the fussiness, the pain. 

Triple feeding (breast, bottle, pump) every feed, on top of a baby that only wanted me, is probably the hardest thing I’ve ever done. 

So I am proud of me, I am proud of her. And I am proud we’ve almost made it 6 months. And hopefully we still have a long blissful journey ahead 💛

I see mums every single day who needed to give formula to their babies (or so they were told) without being told to start pumping. In some cases this may lead to engorged breasts, blocked ducts, mastitis and ultimately low supply when the body doesn’t receive the right signals to make enough milk. This is why, when there is a need to supplement, it is crucial to start pumping in order to provide the breast with extra stimulation and efficient milk removal.

I SAID WHAT I SAID — let me explain! 🚨🚩🚩

Let’s dive deeper into the triple feeding hustle—a routine that many breastfeeding parents find themselves caught in, often out of desperation to increase milk supply (and often recommended by a well-intentioned provider) and/or ensure baby’s weight gain. 🔄🍼⁣

Here’s the scoop: Triple feeding—nursing, supplementing with pumped milk or formula, and then pumping—can feel like a relentless cycle, leaving you exhausted and drained both physically and emotionally. 😓⁣

Instead of spinning your wheels with triple feeding, let’s explore some alternative tactics that can help alleviate the burden and promote a more sustainable breastfeeding journey. ⁣

Consider using a manual pump instead of an electric pump to reduce the time spent pumping and to encourage more efficient, quick milk removal. Another thought is to try pumping 30-60 minutes after nursing a few times per day (instead of every single feed) to take advantage of your body’s natural milk production cycle. 🕒🤱⁣

If supplementing with bottles, enlist the help of your partner or a friend to handle feedings, allowing you to focus on rest and recovery. 💖⁣

But MOST IMPORTANTLY -  seek individualized support from a lactation professional! Sometimes well-intentioned providers suggest triple feeding without offering follow-up or alternative solutions, leaving parents feeling overwhelmed and discouraged. Working on individual solutions can help you identify underlying issues, fine-tune your breastfeeding technique, and develop a more SUSTAINABLE feeding plan. 🌟⁣

Remember, breastfeeding is meant to be a nurturing and bonding experience for both you and your baby, not a relentless cycle of feeding and pumping that leaves you drained and defeated. By exploring aternative tactics and seeking support, you can find a more balanced and fulfilling approach to nourishing your little one AND nourish yourself. 💪💖⁣

[ad]  So it turns out that you can have a special interest in breastfeeding medicine, be training towards your IBCLC and have lots of extra knowledge and skills with breastfeeding management - and still have a baby who doesn’t know how to breastfeed, and a body whose anatomy and physiology are slow to get on board with milk production.  So.  Frustrating. 

We’re in the early days still, but have been battling with milk being slow to come in, a baby with jaundice and >10% weight loss who has been too sleepy to latch and feed well, and some breast refusal.

When in this situation, it seems really overwhelming but the management comes back to a few simple principles. 
1) Feed the baby.  Baby needs volume and calories to grow, as well as clear the jaundice and become less sleepy to optimise feeding.  We are using my own expressed milk as well as donor breastmilk from a friend, but formula definitely has a role here too if extra human milk is unavailable.  We are using a mixture of top ups at the breast using a supply line/ supplemental nursing system, as well as a bottle with over bottle feeds (I’ll cover both in more detail later). 

2) Protect the milk supply.  Milk being removed from the breasts stimulates more milk to be produced.  If baby isn’t feeding effectively, using hand expression or a breast pump to remove more milk after feeds is really important.  We were lucky to be gifted a BelleMa Effective Pro by the lovely @morethanmilknz which has been invaluable over this time!  I’m also taking domperidone to try to increase my prolactin levels. 

3) Enjoy the baby and look after the mum (or breastfeeding parent). The “triple feeding” regime of breastfeed-top up-pump is GRUELLING and should only ever be a short term thing - make an exit plan with your LC/ midwife/ doctor so you are not stuck.  It’s also really important to prioritise baby cuddles (especially skin to skin!), sleep, nutrition and hydration, as well as small things to help your own mental health like having a shower or getting out of the house for a walk.  Popping baby in a carrier can help free up your hands and let you move around which means you feel less trapped.  You’ve got this.

The top-up trap.

A large proportion of the breastfeeding support I do is to help families get out of the Top Up Trap. 

The top up trap defined: Parents feel there is not enough milk (or someone suggests there isn't enough if there are weight issues), parents give formula, baby feels over full and sleeps more, baby comes to the breast less, breasts then make less milk because they are being stimulated less frequently, which means parents lose even more confidence in milk supply and the cycle continues and spirals.

Topping up is started for all sorts of reasons: blood sugar issues, weight loss issues, not enough weight gain issues, misunderstanding normal newborn behaviours like cluster feeding, society, scheduled feeds, routines, lack of confidence in breastfeeding and lack of support. 

Some of these babies genuinely need top ups, but so often, parents are not supported with what to do next, how to tell if the baby continues to need extra milk and how to stop! How milk production works is not explained, and pumping some of this wxtra milk to protect supply is often not discussed, so essential if the goal is to exclusively breastfeed.

Some babies do not even need top ups in the first place, and with good information and support, the parents would have understood how to tell that baby was, in fact, getting enough milk. 

So if you have found yourself in this position, topping up after all or most feeds and don't know how to stop, please seek some breastfeeding support to help you bring it back on course. IBCLCs and breastfeeding counsellors are very experienced at helping people in this scenario.

Breastfeeding is half science and half art. The principles of that science are the same for every person, but sometimes the experimental design looks a little different when put into practice. The art of breastfeeding is as varied as art itself. We have all been given different tools, materials, and education on how to use those tools and materials. Trying to exactly copy someone else’s work will be frustrating if you don’t have the same resources. But there can be joy in learning to use what you do have. In the end, our breastfeeding journey could look like a Renoir or a Picasso. Both are beautiful and powerful in their own, unique way. To compare them and see one as “better” than the other is to wrongfully discredit the artist. And to discredit the art is to fail to realize that the masterpiece you have created is your child. 

Your breastfeeding journey is supposed to look like YOUR breastfeeding journey. Don’t worry if it doesn’t look like some one else’s.  Whether breast milk is some, part, or all of your child’s nutrition, keep creating. Be proud of what you’re creating and don’t let anyone’s opinion about your art matter except yours. 

Breastfeeding is half science and half art. But not science like chemistry where measurements need to be precise and mistakes can be made. Science like architecture. Every child needs a nutritional foundation and beams to support their growth and development. You as a parent are that foundation regardless of how or what you chose to feed your child. Whether some, part, or all of your baby’s nutrition, breast milk is building a strong structure. What that structure looks like is dependent on genetics, personality, and parenting.

I'm so excited to share that I have finally published a paper from my MSc. research in UCD on women's experiences of breastfeeding with primary low milk supply. It was important to me to have the research peer-reviewed and published in an academic journal, because that means that the findings can be used to inform policies, guidelines and practices around the provision of support for mothers breastfeeding with primary low milk supply. This was my goal when I decided 4 years ago that I wanted to undertake this research.

This paper concluded that

● breastfeeding mothers with primary low milk supply (PLMS) may experience a range of emotions such as guilt, anger, sadness, anxiety and disappointment 
● women with PLMS may experience acute anxiety - for some this anxiety was so great that they feared they would lose custody of their babies
● the combination of having PLMS and triple feeding can have a detrimental impact on a mother's mental health
● triple feeding can completely dominate a mother's life in the postpartum period and even get in the way of her being able to enjoy and bond with her baby
● mothers with PLMS struggled to find help and support and were frustrated by conflicting information from HCPs
● mothers with PLMS need clear, non-judgemental and evidence-based information from HCPs and IBCLCs on the use of infant formula 

HCPs and IBCLCs need to give greater consideration to a mother's emotional wellbeing and mental health when providing support for PLMS. They also need to acknowledge the embodied desire to breastfeed that some mother have. HCPs and IBCLCs should address the PLMS in antenatal breastfeeding classes, and they should receive training on PLMS and how to provide sensitive and individualised support.

Triple feeding is a TEMPORARY plan many families use when lactation doesn’t go as expected in the early days and weeks postpartum. It may be used when there is low supply or baby is not latching well. It involves three parts to feeding:
1. Latching baby, often for a set amount of time
2. Feeding the baby with either pumped milk or formula
3. Pumping to increase or maintain supply

This plan is EXHAUSTING because congratulations you now have unexpected twins: you’re feeding the baby and your pump which doubles the amount of work you’re doing. This should really be done under the care of an IBCLC with an exit plan or directions for how to pivot. 

What you see pictured is one strategy to take the triple feed down to a double feeding. Instead of putting baby to breast and then bottle feeding after, a tube can be used at the breast (with or without a nipple shield) to feed baby the pumped milk or formula while they are latched. This is often called an SNS, or supplemental nursing system. Pumping is usually still recommended to facilitate milk supply, but baby has access to additional milk at the breast to help streamline feeding. 

If you’re on a triple feeding plan, why? Is it truly from the maternal side because of low supply? Find the root. Is it from a medication or thyroid issue or a blood loss from birth? Targeting those should see an increase in supply and a decrease in the need to pump and supplement. Is it from a poorly feeding baby? Have ties been assessed and addressed? Is baby a preemie but nearing full term? If a baby is not feeding well from the breast and there is plenty of milk, this is not a parent issue but a baby issue that needs appropriately managed. While using a tube at the breast to supplement can make triple feeding easier for some, finding the root and addressing it to wean from the triple feeding is crucial.

Chronic low milk supply (CLMS) and erectile dysfunction (ED) are health conditions with a similar prevalence in people of similar ages. They also share an association with common health issues including metabolic syndrome, diabetes and high blood pressure. Both conditions can impact mental health. And if left unaddressed, both can be harbingers for poor long-term health outcomes.

Yet despite these similarities, CLMS and ED diverge dramatically when it comes to treatments, research and funding. Consider the following:

- ED has 4 FDA-approved medications to treat; CLMS has 0.

- There are 7x more publications in PubMed.gov related to ED than to low milk supply or lactation insufficiency.

- ED is a defined condition with clinical guidelines and best practices for diagnosis and treatment. CLMS has none of these things.

- In 2016 alone, Pfizer made $1.6 billion from Viagra sales (this doesn’t even include profits for the other ED drugs available). By contrast, in 2017, NIH funding for research into all topics related to Breastfeeding, Lactation and Breast Milk was just 5.75% of that.

We can do better. And women/people assigned female at birth who experience CLMS deserve better!

If we spent even a tenth of 1 year of profits for ED drugs on research into treatments for CLMS, this picture would be different.

It’s time to kill the myth that “some people just can’t” and start finding solutions. If we can do it for ED, we can do it for CLMS.

It’s World Breastfeeding Week and in the spirit of keeping it real, I wanted to share what it’s been like for us so far. I was prepared for it to be difficult - all my friends & research had warned me of that. I was prepared to struggle through the mechanics of BFing, for it to be painful, for it not to come effortlessly. But what I wasn’t prepared for, was that I simply wouldn’t produce enough milk to feed my baby. I’ve struggled with a low milk supply right out of the gate. Was it from the stress of the pregnancy rash and nearly two months of broken sleep leading up to the birth? Was it because of my long and somewhat traumatizing labor? Was it because me & Lux were separated right after he was born? Was my hypothyroidism playing a role? Was it because the baby wasn’t latching well & signaling my body to produce more? Was it a combination of everything? We’ll never know exactly why, or what caused it. I did all the right things to fix it though: worked with a lactation consultant, did triple feedings to stimulate production, power pumping, ate enough, drank enough water, supplemented with electrolyte powders, lactation herbs, teas, and cookies, even went to the extreme of having a lip and tongue tie revision done on Lux to help him latch better and pull more milk. Some days I produce a little more milk and think we may be starting to turn the corner but it’s still only about a third of what he needs. When Lux was just a few days old, I could tell he was getting dehydrated from the lack of wet diapers and I asked our pediatrician about supplementing with formula and she made a suggestion to try using donor milk instead. Donor milk?? You mean feed my baby with another woman’s breastmilk? (continued in comments)

Whether it’s 3, 5, or 10% of the population, there are people that struggle to or never make a full breast milk supply. From 1 month to 1 year, exclusively breastfed babies average 25oz of breast milk per day. True low milk supply means making less than this when the breasts are stimulated every 1-3 hours day and night. Chronic low milk supply is linked to either a greater health concern or something out of your control which you cannot change or fix with cookies, teas or even sometimes medications and pumping.

🗝Low milk supply that can be increased with time and support:
💡Baby not feeding efficiently from lack of oral motor skill or tongue tie
💡Taking certain prescription medications with a side effect of dropping milk (Sudafed, Benadryl, antibiotics)
💡Not feeding or pumping enough, especially over night
💡Scheduled feedings or over use of a pacifier
💡Birth. Many medications designed to help you labor and deliver actually inhibit baby from latching and feeding effectively for hours to days after birth. Hemorrhage or birth trauma can also cause low supply in the beginning
💡Supplementing, especially in the two weeks after birth

🗝Reasons for chronic low milk supply that may increase even with maximal support:
💡Insufficient glandular tissue (IGT) Breasts never developed during puberty and look tubular or widely spaced. Signs of IGT include breasts did not grow in puberty, or increase in size during pregnancy. No engorgement in the week after birth
💡Uncontrolled or undiagnosed thyroid disorder
💡Uncontrolled diabetes
💡Hormone or endocrine disorders, including severe PCOS
💡Hormonal birth control placed/used too soon after delivery
💡Breast or nipple surgery, augmentation, reduction, trauma
💡Nipple piercing that scars shut instead of staying open
There is a mistaken belief that prescription galactagogues, teas, or herbs can cure ANY chronic low milk supply. Before self-prescribing or taking Domperidone, Reglan, fenugreek, or any other lactation supplement, consider having your serum prolactin levels tested and a full evaluation by a skilled lactation consultant

If we’ve heard it once, we’ve heard it a thousand times: “When I asked my doctor to help me understand why I have low supply, they told me that ‘some women just don’t make enough.’”

THIS IS NOT ACCEPTABLE. For what other medical condition is “we don’t know and we won’t even look” an adequate answer? 

Some men can’t get an erection...but that triggers a complete work up to examine possible metabolic and cardiovascular issues.

Some people can’t make enough insulin to control their blood sugar...but that triggers an investigation of possible diabetes.

Some people can’t see very well...but that triggers a comprehensive eye and/or neurological examination.

It is true that some of the underlying causes of low milk supply cannot be corrected quickly, if at all. But that DOES NOT mean that those parents don’t deserve the time and support from their medical providers to understand what is going on in their bodies.

Breastfeeding is half science and half art. The principles of that science are the same for every person, but sometimes the experimental design looks a little different when put into practice. The art of breastfeeding is as varied as art itself. We have all been given different tools, materials, and education on how to use those tools and materials. Trying to exactly copy someone else’s work will be frustrating if you don’t have the same resources. But there can be joy in learning to use what you do have. In the end, our breastfeeding journey could look like a Renoir or a Picasso. Both are beautiful and powerful in their own, unique way. To compare them and see one as “better” than the other is to wrongfully discredit the artist. And to discredit the art is to fail to realize that the masterpiece you have created is your child. 

Your breastfeeding journey is supposed to look like YOUR breastfeeding journey. Don’t worry if it doesn’t look like some one else’s.  Whether breast milk is some, part, or all of your child’s nutrition, keep creating. Be proud of what you’re creating and don’t let anyone’s opinion about your art matter except yours. 

Breastfeeding is half science and half art. But not science like chemistry where measurements need to be precise and mistakes can be made. Science like architecture. Every child needs a nutritional foundation and beams to support their growth and development. You as a parent are that foundation regardless of how or what you chose to feed your child. Whether some, part, or all of your baby’s nutrition, breast milk is building a strong structure. What that structure looks like is dependent on genetics, personality, and parenting.

Low milk supply is about more than just how much milk a person makes. Studies show that parents who encounter breast/chestfeeding difficulties are more likely to struggle with postpartum depression and anxiety as well. In a world where the benefits of human milk are emphasized over and over, the pain of not making enough to feed your baby (even when triple feeding and taking every galactagogue under the sun!) should not be underestimated.

It can be hard to know what to say when someone shares that they have chronic low milk supply, especially since this condition is not prominent or well understood. In our experience, the urge that people have to help is often expressed through questions and suggestions. While these may come from a place of care, they can feel very invalidating to a parent with CLMS. It is extremely frustrating having to explain that you have already tried these suggestions (and usually more!) to no avail. 

So what's the best way to respond? By providing support, affirmation of their experience and acceptance of their choices about their body and how they feed their baby. If you're in a position to do so, it's also great to help them advocate for their health, since often doctors are not any better informed about the causes of and tests associated with CLMS. Your support can make a huge difference in helping that parent overcome the difficult and emotionally devastating experience of CLMS.

One of the most difficult parts of dealing with chronic low milk supply are the emotions that come with it. Parents describe feeling shocked that this could happen to them; angry that no one warned them low supply was possible; inadequate because they must supplement to feed their babies; devastated that they have tried everything possible to increase supply without success. Experiencing these emotions at a time when hormones are already running high (and sleep is at an all-time low!) can be especially overwhelming. 

But chronic low milk supply isn’t something that you have to face alone. Find resources and support at www.lowmilksupplyfoundation.org/parents.

Breastfeeding Bandaids can be needed, but should always be a short term solution while the root cause of the issue is figured out.⁠ Bandaids can help symptoms but not solve problems. 
⁠
🔶NIPPLE SHIELDS:⁠
Nipple shields are often used when a baby can't latch or when there is pain with latching.  Neither situation is normal and the cause should be figured out in order to make a plan to get off the nipple shield.⁠
⁠
🔶PUMPING AFTER BREASTFEEDS⁠
Sometimes parents pump after feeds at the breast in order to increase supply so the baby has more easy milk.  Again, this can be effective short term, but the baby should be able to maintain milk supply on his own and often there are simple solutions to help baby do this and decrease that workload for mama.⁠
⁠
🔶TRIPLE FEEDING⁠
Triple feeding is when you feed at the breast, pump and then feed that milk back either via bottle, finger feeding, cup feeding etc.  Triple feeding, like other bandaids, can be needed short term.  However, it is too much work to be a long term solution. ⁠
⁠
🔶REFLUX MEDS⁠
True acid reflux in babies is rare and usually only seen in preterm babies.  More commonly I see reflux due to swallowing air either because of a bad latch or because of an uncoordinated swallow OR reflux due to a food sensitivity.  Either way reflux meds are a bandaid to cover up why it is happening and this bandaid is not benign.  These meds were never studied on babies for safety, but retrospective research has shown that when given as a baby, they increase the baby's chances of broken bones as a child.⁠
⁠
🔶NIPPLE CREAM⁠
There are some great and not so great nipple creams out there for damaged nipples, but either way, they shouldn't be relied upon long term to keep pain or damage at bay. 
⁠
If you are using a bandaid and want to stop, find someone that is willing to dig in the weeds with you and figure out the root cause and also a way to fix that root cause!⁠

2 things that are associated but are not the same thing. 

From 16+ weeks ➡️ day 3ish after birth your body makes colostrum. It’s a sticky yellow thick milk that is hyper-concentrated with immune cells and good bacteria. It needs to be a small volume to coat the baby’s GI tract + seed the microbiome + protect baby from infections. 

By day 3 your body has understood that the baby is born (your progesterone plummets)- resulting in cellular changes that increase volume of milk. This is called secretory activation. You may or may not notice a fuller breast and swallowing sounds are louder!

Sometimes, the milk transition is delayed. I used the mute button here- because the signal for volume is off. This delay is predictable based on your pregnancy and birth story. Unfortunately, many families are not being informed that this does NOT mean low milk production! However, when supplements and pumping start, now milk removal is dependent on a pump not the baby’s needs and there will be a production mis-match. It’s hard to pump AND care for a baby so parents will struggle and feel guilty about their inability to pump so frequently and produce the volume their baby drinks. 
Parents also do not get discharged with appropriate lactation follow up to stop pumping! And they burn out and many stop breastfeeding within the first month. 

Low production happens when there is less milk removed from the breast- ex: the baby can’t latch well / pump isn’t removing milk well / mom can’t pump frequently enough or doesn’t have the medical care to stop pumping. 

Other reasons can be anatomical, like less glandular (milk making) tissue from development or surgery or hormonal reasons- I used the volume symbol here! 

Secretory Activation and low production are related yes, but not the same. 

We can identify these women at risk of delay of secretory activation and prevent them from burning out with a pump and prevent the low production with evidence based lactation management.

Triple feeding is not a sustainable (or sane) long-term feeding plan!

Triple feeding is (1) breastfeeding the baby, (2) pumping, and (3) feeding the baby either pumped milk or formula supplement within the same feeding session. It’s physically and mentally EXHAUSTING. By the time you finish feeding, pumping, and cleaning, it’s time to feed all over again. It can also lead to oversupply in some people.

This is a short-term strategy to increase supply — it should ALWAYS include a plan with an off ramp. 

If a pediatrician or lactation professional instructed you to triple feed without providing you with a follow-up plan to move away from it — that ain’t right! 

Here’s how to triple feed in a healthy way:

- Trial triple feeding for one week before re-evaluating
- Make SURE you have support at home. It’s not possible to do this and also care for a baby by yourself 
- Don’t feel like you need to triple feed for every single feeding, aim for at least 4-6 per day, or consider power pumping at the end of the day to replace some pumping sessions. Make sure to remove milk overnight as well, but consider pumping while your partner feeds so you can get back to sleep more quickly
- Looking to move away from triple feeding and not sure how? Contact a reputable/trusted lactation professional and ask them for a specific plan (best if this can be based on a consultation with a weighted breastfeed in conjunction with serial baby weight checks)

Posted @withregram • @kellyibclc This position for paced bottle feeding is great for babies under 3 months old.  Paced bottle feeding is important for those going back and forth between breast and bottle.  However, I find that sitting them upright doesn't work well for all babies, especially tinies because they don't have enough support for their bodies.  I find that sometimes when parents or caregivers are trying to sit up newborns to pace bottle feed, the newborn collapses in and then isn't in a good position to feed.  This solves that problem. 

Reasons to Pace Bottle Feed:
💧You can keep a baby from eating too quickly and overfeeding
💧Baby is able to regulate their suck, swallow, breath pattern without milk dripping in their mouth
💧Baby can regulate their own feed
💧You can pace the feed similar to the pace at the breast
💧Baby will not prefer bottle flow to the breast flow - especially when milk supply isn't huge.  Humans will always choose the path of least resistance and if it's way easier to drink from a bottle, they will choose it even if, in the end, easier does not mean better for them.

Other things to think about when pacing the feed.
🍼Hold the bottle horizontal
🍼Make sure their chin is not tucked down toward their chest
🍼If they are going back and forth between breast and bottle, don't give them milk right away.  Make them work for it.  Tip the bottle down a bit, so there is no milk in the nipple. They should suck suck suck for at least 10 seconds before they are rewarded with milk.  When at the breast, it typically takes at least that long to elicit a let down.  This makes it so they do not expect milk right away at breast and keeps frustrations at bay. 
🍼Take breaks throughout the feed by tipping the bottle slightly down.

"It is estimated that 5–15% of breastfeeding parents experience chronic lactation insufficiency. Given the ∼3.6 million live births in the United States in 2020, we can extrapolate that this issue affected anywhere from 180,000 to >500,000 breastfeeding dyads in the past year alone. These parents are not able to feed their children the biologically optimal source of nutrition for infants, nor are they able to follow breastfeeding recommendations from major health organizations such as the World Health Organization, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the American Academy of Pediatrics. The children of parents affected by chronic lactation insufficiency are also possibly missing the immune system benefits afforded by breastfeeding—a lack acutely felt during the COVID-19 pandemic. Finally, parents who plan to breastfeed and find themselves unable to do so often feel betrayed by their bodies. They may feel judged by family, peers, and health care providers, and hopeless about their lack of choice in how they feed their infants. This mélange of emotions may increase the risk for postpartum mood disorders, another growing public health concern."

Let’s talk about the “C” in Chronic Low Milk Supply (CLMS) and why the terminology we use matters. 

If you’re a parent with low milk supply and you’ve discussed your supply issues with anyone, you’ve probably been advised to try common interventions like increased pumping/nursing, more skin-to-skin, different size flanges, herbal galactagogues, prescription medication and more. 

While this advice is well-meaning, it’s important to realize that for 10-15% of lactating parents, these interventions will not lead to a full supply because the cause(s) of their low supply are more complex.

It’s also important to note that often, these parents have already tried all of these suggestions (and more!).

By using the terminology “chronic low milk supply,” the LMSF seeks to clearly delineate CLMS as a type of low milk supply that does not respond to common interventions; is likely related to an underlying health condition and/or lack of glandular tissue; and that requires a deep and nuanced understanding of the causes of low supply in order to be properly addressed. 

We also want to empower parents with CLMS to quickly signal to medical providers, lactation professionals and others that their low supply is a medical concern, not a management issue.

For more information about how to approach CLMS, visit our website (link in bio)!

Thankfully awareness of non-IgE allergies is becoming more common-which means more parents are getting the support they need to manage them. This type of allergy can be hard to diagnose and manage especially in little bubs.

Unfortunately, we do have the highest rates of food allergy in Australia with 1 in 10 infants having a food allergy. 

The really tricky thing is that a lot of the symptoms we see in non-IgE allergy are also similar to “normal newborn fusiness” and the spectrum of what is “normal” for baby poo can also make it confusing for parents. 

I have lost count of the number of parents I have seen that were told that their baby was just “purple crying” and that it was usual behaviour to be crying all day and night. That as long as they are gaining weight gain “it’s okay”…..Yes- some babies are more unsettled as they find their way in the world (it is a lot to get use to!) but if you also see this alongside other symptoms we have flagged I would really suggest you look into support to explore food allergy or intolerance. 

Lastly- even if it isn’t an underlying medical condition causing your little one to be more unhappy this doesn’t mean you don’t need or deserve support. Babies need us deeply and some babies need a lot more support than others. This in turn means we need to be supporting these parents more. So no matter the “why” behind “why” you’re having a hard time- ask for help and support. Find a GP that listens and gets to know your family. See your Maternal Child Health Nurse and ask what supports are available. Talk to a lactation consultant if breastfeeding isn’t feeling right. Chat to a dietitian if you think food is an issue before you start cutting anything out.

Fed is best. Whether you breastfeed, pump, formula feed or a combination - if your baby is fed you are doing this whole mom thing right!!!
•
1.Take a BF class during your third trimester and bring your spouse; it is so important to lay the groundwork before baby’s birth (a *lot* to learn!). This class will cover the latch, BF positions, and baby’s “feeding cues”
2.After birth, it will take TIME; I’m 99% sure BF does not come natural nor easy for anyone. It takes a few weeks for you and baby to figure this out; try not to get frustrated and just keep trying
3.Have the hospital’s Lactation Consultant help you with the latch as many times as possible before you leave
4.Be proactive with pumping (if ok’d with the hospital LC) - they had me pumping 15-20min by day 2
5.Have bottles sterilized and ready to go when you come home, just in case. I didn’t plan on introducing a bottle so early, so all my bottles were still in boxes. We had to since she lost 13% of her birthweight and were #triplefeeding
6.Ensure you have breastmilk storage containers for refrigerator and freezer 
7.When you are starting out, put a warm compress on your breasts for 3-5 min and lightly massage to get things going (I used the same small compresses from my PIO injections; Thrive heat packs, Amazon)
8.Have a comfortable chair to sit in while feeding your baby; the nursery glider worked way better for me than in my bed propped up with pillows
9.Under the Affordable Care Act (US), health insurance companies are required to provide you with a breast pump; get yours for free and do not add this pricey item to your registry. I like the #medelapumpinstyle
10.BF support and free resources: @lalecheleagueusa is nationwide and most cities have additional local & hospital groups
11.Have a #boppypillow and nipple cream(s) on hand! You will use these things 8+ times a day!!

Since the second day in the hospital after our twins were born, we were #triplefeeding the twins (breastfeeding, bottle feeding with pumped milk/donor milk and pumping) and working with #lactationeducation specialists. This had been a goal of mine all along - but it's not easy and I wasn't sure if I could do it - but I did it! This has been critical to getting the twins on the same feeding/sleeping schedule, which allows @kunkuwana and me to get the most sleep possible at this stage. The alternative is that we would be breast/bottle feeding literally around the clock, which was what we had been doing, and it was exhausting! We occasionally give them bottles of pumped milk/donor milk, but at this point, I am able to feed the twins primarily at the breast, which has been incredibly positive for all of us!

"I was 100% confident in my ability to create a full supply, despite my baby being in the NICU. Even pumping seven to eight times per day on the advice of hospital LCs, I couldn't."

When hormonal issues are compounded with birth trauma, separation from baby, and other complications, it can feel like a wild goose chase trying to pin down the root cause of low supply. Poor advice, vaguely explained supplementation practices, and being told to triple feed indefinitely only compound the problem, leading to many regrets and "what ifs." 

New parents don't know what they don't know. It's important for providers to offer appropriate guidance, with holistic physical and mental health in mind, rather than blanket statements about pumping more and adding 2 ounces of formula at every feed. Resources for parents and providers are key to our mission, so everyone gets the individualized healthcare they need.

Triple feeding, ie pumping, bottle feeding AND breastfeeding, a lot of work and should rarely be a longterm solution to a breastfeeding problem. Most women find it unsustainable. I see a lot of clients who have been told to triple feed - breastfeed for 15 minutes on each breast, top baby up with a bottle, and then double pump for  20 minutes - into infinity and beyond. Often there is no time frame given to this strategy, no end point discussed, eg "do this until.....". I know it's not always possible to definitively state when triple feeding should stop, but women need to be reassured that it's not forever, and only part of a longer term plan. 
If you are triple feeding, talk with whoever is supporting you with breastfeeding about 
- the timeframe. How long are you going to do this for?
- what is manageable for you? 8 pumps a day? 5 pumps a day? 3 pumps a day? It has to be manageable. 
- what's the goal? increasing milk supply? waiting until baby is feeding more effectively at the breast? how will you know when you have reached the goal? 
- are there alternatives to triple pumping? 
- what do you really want?

A Lactation Consultant should be supportive all feeding methods! ⁣
⁣
✨ Yes our specialty is breastfeeding, but that doesn’t mean that LC’s should be mean, judgmental, or non supportive of families that choose not to breastfeed! (And they shouldn’t try to persuade them to breastfeed).⁣
⁣
✨ When I first went into this profession fresh from taking my IBCLC board exam, my LC mentor @janiyamwilliams_ taught me that formula was not bad. She also taught me that the breastfeeding parent’s emotional health and a fed baby was more important. ⁣
⁣
✨ I was taught how to assess breast anatomy and medical history in relation to breastfeeding. I was also taught how to identify signs of low milk supply and inform families of multiple feeding options that would work best for their needs so they can make an informed choice. She was the first LC I knew that practiced this way and I’m forever grateful to have had her as a mentor. ⁣
⁣
✨ Exclusive breastfeeding does not work for everyone. Your Lactation Consultant should be able to assess what your feeding goals are and then do a thorough medical and breast history. ⁣
⁣
✨ From there you should be presented with realistic feeding options that are specific for you and your baby’s needs. You should be able to make an INFORMED choice on how you want to feed your baby without judgement. Ideally this should happen prenatally. ⁣
⁣
✨ My heart really hurts when I hear of stories of LC’s that were not supportive or not realistic of parent’s feeding goals and decisions. ⁣
⁣

T R I P L E  F E E D I N G

Triple feeding is when you breastfeed, then pump, then bottle feed. It is very exhausting and very time consuming. Usually triple feeding is recommended to help boost moms milk supply or to help with baby’s weight gain.

Perhaps baby isn’t transferring well and is not removing the milk effectively therefore compromising mom’s milk supply. Whatever you pump, you would give to your baby afterwards to help with weight gain.

While triple feeding demands your body to make more milk, it’s also very time consuming. You nurse for 20-40minutes, then pump for 20mins then you have to bottle feed which you can either hand off to someone else, or you spend another 15minutes bottle feeding. Then you have about an hour break before you do it all over again 😅

Well one recommendation I give moms, is to pump WHILE you’re nursing. You put your baby on one side while you pump the other. You can then bottle/cup/or spoon feed your baby the milk you pumped. It’s like killing two birds with one stone.

To do this, I recommend 1️⃣getting a hands free pumping bra like @medela_us Or @simplewisheshandsfree 2️⃣Get the bra and pump situated first. 3️⃣Pull one side of the bra below your breast that you plan on nursing on. 4️⃣Latch your baby and 5️⃣turn the pump on.

Studies have found that double breast stimulation yields more milk, an extra let down, and even a higher fat content!

Like 85% of women, I planned to breastfeed my baby. 

By the time I was pregnant with my first baby, I was already a pediatrician. I thought I had a good idea of what breastfeeding would be like. Sure, there may be some challenges but nothing I couldn’t work through, right?

I was wrong. The first 6 weeks of learning to breastfeed turned out to be the most challenging 6 weeks of my life— more difficult than any stretch of medical school or residency. It was full of pain, pumping, crying (both me and baby), leaking, and refusing. 

What would I tell myself if I could go back in time? 

Have your resources and support lined up before you deliver. Anticipate that there are going to be issues and know exactly who to call when they happen! And have multiple resources to call. When I tried to get an appointment with a lactation consultant, the earliest appointment was 5 weeks away 😳

I would also tell myself to set small goals. My initial goal was to breastfeed for one year, but after my daughter was a week old, the thought of doing it for a year was too daunting. My goal changed to one month, and at one month I reassessed and the new goal became 2 months, and so on. It was much easier to have a goal that seemed within reach during those trying first weeks.

If you are in the midst of this struggle right now, know that you are not alone!

It’s been said before, but bears repeating: breastfeeding doesn’t have to be all or nothing! And even with low milk supply, it’s still possible to have a successful breastfeeding experience and take pride in your journey. 

This was the case for Desiree. After learning she was pregnant with her first child, “I was thrilled at the idea of being a breastfeeding mom,” Desiree remembers. “I read what felt like every book and article in existence and prepared myself with every tool known to mom: a pump, nursing pads, nursing pillow, nursing bras, manual pumps, Haakaas, the works. I threw out any formula sample I got, as well as the coupons, because I had no intention of ever using it.”

At her daughter’s first check-up, however, Desiree got the devastating news that she was not making enough to support healthy weight gain in her baby. “I began triple feeding with the help of my husband at every feed. It was thoroughly exhausting, both physically and mentally. I cried at almost every bottle I had to give her and every pump I had to do,” Desiree says.

With the help of a strict pumping regimen and Reglan, Desiree increased her supply to about half of her baby’s intake. More importantly, she found a way to redefine what breastfeeding success looked like for her. “I stopped pumping after feeds and just nursed and supplemented around the clock using the supplemental nursing system (SNS) or following with a bottle. After a long time of doing this, I found peace with my journey and maintained a strong nursing bond with my daughter until she weaned at about 1.5 years old.”

Every lactation journey is different, and every parent who wants to breastfeed deserves the support and encouragement they need to find success, whatever that looks like for them.

If you have a story about success with breastfeeding through low supply, we’d love to hear it in the comments!

Fact: breast milk is superior to any other substance for babies. 

Myth: how long or if you feed your baby breast milk is correlated to how good of a mother you are or moral superiority.

Do not internalize this myth. Everyone makes risk based choices. 

I mean whole, organic vegetables and organic, pasture raised meats are the best choice to feed my kids. That’s a fact. 

Does that mean I don’t feed my kids granola bars and processed chicken nuggets? No. I don’t feel the anywhere near amount of shame that mothers are made to feel about their infant feeding choices. The fact that it’s better is just a fact. 

Own your choices and don’t let others make you feel shame ✨🤍✨

The physiology of making milk tells us that to make milk, milk needs to be removed from the breast often. 

When the baby latches well, that’s usually all that is needed. 

When the baby can’t latch well, then we need something else to remove milk- enter the breast pump.

Commonly what happens is in the first 2 weeks your baby may be not feeding well for a variety of reasons the most common are: 

Preterm
Jaundice
Injury
Low sugars
Other health reasons
Learning
Mom isn’t well
Breast swelling 

And if this happens parents are told to supplement (feed another way) and then pump. Parents often don’t understand the reason behind their need to supplement and pump - and when they can stop, wean and how etc. 

When supplementing and pumping starts, parents also become more concerned about their infants wellbeing and they have less trust and confidence in breastfeeding. 

Your baby’s reason for not feeding well may be past ( jaundice resolved!) yet you may question if it’s really ok to stop offering a bottle after breastfeeds. 

Pumping after every feed becomes exhausting and unsustainable-

Parents need to be INFORMED about why they need supplementation and then offered support and lactation care to get back to breastfeeding if that’s their intention. 

Pumping is an INTERVENTION that is needed sometimes. 

But if your baby can latch comfortably and they are healthy and growing well, and back to birth weight you can use the baby to help remove the milk. 

How? 

✅ increase skin to skin 
✅ switch sides when swallows stop to encourage more let downs and milk transfer
✅ breast compressions 
✅ offer your breast more often for more opportunity to get milk 
✅ offer your breast for comfort and sleep. All that stimulation helps! 
✅ Respond to your baby by feeding your baby on cue and give baby control with bottles by paced bottle feeding. 
✅ limit pumping to when you are using a bottle only, and baby isn’t latching at all. 
✅ stay close to baby (babywear) so you can see their early feeding cues, they stay calmer and they smell your milk. 
✅ supplement at breast 

If you are pumping and want to stop but are worried about losing supply or baby not eating enough-seek help.

Sometimes babies will move up or down a bit but still track on their curve. CHOP.edu says a "downward change in growth across two major growth percentiles" is Failure to Thrive.

Many times we see families who had falling percentiles for months that were dismissed until their baby was below the 5th percentile. It's SO much less work for you if you identify the cause as soon as possible so you can correct it. 

Weight doesn't stabilize by magic. Early intervention with an IBCLC is key. 

Bonus fact: Excessive sleepiness is a symptom of Failure to Thrive. SO MANY TIMES these babies are praised for being "great sleepers" when they're really conserving energy 😔

Often, one of the first major clues a parent has that they have low supply is a precipitous drop in baby’s weight. This can be exacerbated by the common advice of “just keep putting baby to breast” if the baby is burning too many calories while trying to nurse. That was exactly the situation in which first-time parent Huda found herself. “When my baby was five days old we had to rush her to the ER because of severe jaundice and she had to be kept under the lights for 24 hours. I was told that it was because I had low milk supply, and she was starving. That made sense to me later, since at night she would only sleep for half an hour at a time and constantly be latched for hours and then cry!”

Unfortunately, Huda received little support or information about how to best sustain her supply while giving her baby the necessary supplementation. Instead, she was advised to eat oatmeal and pump more. “Pump, pump, pump and you’ll make enough milk” was something I heard way too many times,” she says. 

Even as baby gained weight, Huda was too afraid to nurse for long. “[I wish someone told me I] should latch the baby on as much as possible when she was not as hungry and top off with a bottle, and not chase numbers or ounces in the bottle,” Huda reflects. 

Parents like Huda who experience low supply should receive the support they need to understand their options. Even when supplementation is required to support weight gain, it’s still possible to keep baby at breast, maintain (and even increase) supply and meet your breastfeeding goals!

UNEXPECTED PUMP LIFE ✨ 

My plan was to exclusively breastfeed at least for the first month of my baby’s life. We had bottles, a warmer, and a bottle rack, but I didn’t have them handy, as I thought they were something to worry about way down the line. I hadn’t even picked out my pump yet, and didn’t feel in a rush to do so.

Well, Benjamin coming almost 6 weeks early thrust me into the world of pumping REAL quick. Being that he was premature, his suck & swallow reflex was not yet fully developed, he had trouble latching, and on top of that, he had a slight tongue tie.

In the hospital, we only had Ben every 3 hours for a mere 30 minutes. It was too stressful to try and get him to latch properly in that short time AND assume he was getting what he needed, so pumping truly was our best option (we had already decided formula would be last resort).

Benny’s first feed was actually the colostrum that I collected during labor to get contractions going again. I had plans to collect my colostrum closer to my due date (lol to that) so I was kind of given that opportunity in a backwards way. 

Pumping did not (and has not) come easy. Despite having lactation consultant guidance in the hospital, I ended up almost having mastitis (but @pumpwithpurpose saved me). I have learned more about pumping in these almost three weeks than I ever thought imaginable. 

I don’t plan on pumping forever, and we are slowly transitioning from bottle to breast, but I am beyond thankful that it’s an option that still gets us to our goal—breast milk.

Moral of this story: don’t be like me and assume you don’t need everything prepped—plan for it ALL. And, most importantly, bottle feeding IS breastfeeding, and you can slap whoever says otherwise ☺️

Have you heard of triple feeding? 

It goes like this:

1. Feed baby at breast
2. Pump
3. Supplement baby pumped breastmilk 

This can be a helpful strategy in some cases, but it’s really only meant to be used for a few days. 

On a weekly basis, mothers walk into my office and tell me they have been doing this for WEEKS! 

Triple Feeding is NOT a long term solution to feeding a baby. It’s exhausting, and in my opinion, not sustainable for a mom and baby. 

Mama, this post isn’t here to tell you you’re doing something wrong. In fact, if you’ve been long term triple feeding, I think you’re a pretty hard core mama bear who is willing to do whatever it takes 😉😘. 

I just want you to know this is a really good reason to reach out to a feeding professional for help! We need to get to the root cause of the problem and come up with a sustainable feeding plan 🤍.

What to do if you have low milk supply after the first couple of months

There will be a point where you may decide that you have maximised your production. This can be quite variable from one person to the next and depends very much on how well baby is feeding. Long term triple feeding is unsustainable so it may be a time to make peace with your production and begin to think about ways to make feeding more sustainable 

If you get to the stage where baby is latching well, having both breasts each feed, actively feeding and you are not able to express any greater volume of milk each 24 hours, this may be the time to reassess and move away from a full triple feeding regime

If you are finding that baby is settled after most breastfeeds and it is more of a slow weight gain issue that is the main symptom of supply, it may be necessary to give a few of bottles of donor milk or formula per day to maintain weight gain and just breastfeed responsively in between

But if you are finding baby is rarely settled after breastfeeds, you may need to give a bit of extra milk each feed. Some choose to offer a bottle feed at the end of the feed. Sometimes giving it mid-feed and settling baby on the breast protects the breastfeeding relationship more effectively. If baby is fussy and refusing to latch, the bottle could be given at the start of the feed and then baby settles on the breast

Another option is to give the extra milk with a tube at the breast, or supplementary nursing system. An SNS protects the breastfeeding relationship as the baby get supplental feed whilst breastfeeding without the need for bottles. Babies that have to have a lot of bottles are at greater risk of eventually rejecting the breast. They can be used for all feeds or some

Expressing is often the part that is least sustainable. And with low supply it may be for a small volume of milk. You may find using some breast compressions or switching back and forth a couple of times may encourage baby to take that milk. Once production is no longer being increased if baby is feeding effectively, expressing can usually be stopped. If baby is not feeding well then it may be prudent to keep some expressing

Weight checks are so stressful. Save these tips to have a successful weight check! 

1. Timing matters. Newborns should gain an average of 1oz per day until they're 4mos. If their last appointment was in the late afternoon and their recheck was in the early morning, that's a whole day's worth of feedings they didn't get to count towards their weight.

2. If your baby was in a clean newborn diaper for the last visit, make sure it's the same for this visit. This is especially important if you use cloth diapers. If your baby has a huge blowout before getting weighed, make sure to let your doctor know. 💩 weighs a lot!

3. DON'T walk into a weight check with a baby who hasn't eaten in 2hrs. Feed them in the car or in the exam room before the weight.

4. Babies should regain their birth weight by 2 weeks. If their weight still isn't trending in a positive direction, you need a plan that's not based on guesses or random numbers. Don't do a weighted feeding in the office, since office scales aren't designed for a newborn weighted feeding in grams. The only way to come up with an appropriate feeding plan is to work with an IBCLC. 

They can help you determine if nursing just needs to be optimized or if your baby needs a supplement. If so, they'll help you figure out how much, with what (syringe, cup, spoon, SNS, bottle), and support you in supplementing with your milk or formula. So often we see babies two weeks in who aren't nursing well or at all because of inappropriate supplementation in the newborn period. Get help BEFORE things go off the rails. We couldn’t let September pass by without discussing Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), one of the leading causes of infertility and a commonly seen disorder among those with chronic low milk supply. 

PCOS is thought to be the most common hormonal disorder among women of childbearing age, affecting as many as 1 in 4 women between the ages of 18 and 44. As a “syndrome,” PCOS can vary in the way it presents; symptoms can also change over time. It is also incredibly underdiagnosed.

PCOS is fundamentally a women’s health issue that can have profound long-term mental and physical health impacts. And it is unacceptable that a condition that affects so many women is so little understood. We must join together to demand better from our healthcare providers, and our healthcare system in general -- better understanding, better research, better support and better treatments!

Sometimes the baby isn’t gaining enough weight, and mom is told to feed baby at the breast then pump then top up with a bottle. This is called triple feeding, because you are doing 3 things every time baby is eating. It also gets mom triple exhausted triple fast. Yup, that’s correct math.

What providers sometimes miss is the WHY. Why is this baby not gaining weight? It is not always because mom is not producing enough milk! In the early days after birth it can be due to factors that make it difficult for baby to transfer the milk from the breast.

Sleepiness (jaundice), shallow latch, not offering enough, tongue tie, jaw asymmetries, tight neck or bottle feeds (these will make the baby full so less likely to latch and eat from mom).

The WHY is the most important part, because if we can correct the reason the baby isn’t getting the milk, we can stop triple feeds.

Triple feeding is a temporary tool to buy some time to figure out the WHY. It keeps the baby fed while the provider makes a plan to get you back to feeding at the breast. Feeding at the breast on demand is the LEAST amount of WORK. We know women who exclusively breastfeed sleep more and have less rates of postpartum depression. Whenever triple feeds begin, we must ask how is it going to end? Sustaining it long term is not realistic. Most parents do not know how to stop triple feeds once they start. See an IBCLC for guidance.

How do I know when to pump?
 
The answer to this is dependent on whether you are using just your milk to top up (1), or whether you are also using formula and whether you want to stop using formula (2 & 3)

Many families find themselves supplementing their baby's feeds with expressed milk or formula in the early days for a various reasons. And most then wish to stop once they have had some breastfeeding support or baby is more physically or developmentally able to exclusively breastfeed.

1) If you are using solely your milk to top up, then you just need to express what baby is taking. A good way to do this is to always have a top up un the fridge. And if you use it, replace it. So if baby has 40ml from a bottle or other way of supplementing, you need to pump 40ml. If you cant pump immediately, try ASAP

2) If you are reluctantly using formula to top up, you'll need to work on your supply. As baby gets more efficient they should need less top up (*if you have an underlying supply issue, please check out my combi/low supply highlight) So the first thing to do is to try to pump to replace some of the formula they are having. Once the combination of baby feeding better and getting more milk directly and you pumping means you are providing all baby's milk then follow step 1

3) If you are using some formula and are happy doing so then as baby needs less top ups you can begin to gradually pump less, as in step 1. Its best to aim to keep formula to 1 or 2 feeds in 24 hours for long term combi feeding, to reduce risk of breast refusal

Some will want to make a stash of milk for future emergencies. This is fine as long as you keep "extra" pumping to a minimum. And you only need one or two feeds in the freezer for a stash unless you know you are going to be away from your baby more than a few hours. So pumping once a day, or even once every few days is enough to make a small stash. Its important not to pump and store large volumes that your baby isn't drinking as this will give you an over supply and put you at increased risk of engorgement, blocked ducts, mastitis, unsettled baby, baby reflux, baby struggling to latch

Early baby? Any reason to supplement? Think triple feeding!

After I had my daughter, who was born a little bit early at 37+5 weeks gestation, breastfeeding was definitely a struggle! Because she was very sleepy and not feeding well, I was told to give her a bottle after breastfeeding. This was indicated, but I was never informed of the crucial step of pumping if a bottle was given. This impacted my milk being delayed coming in and my long term milk supply. 

My story has definitely given me a passion to make sure moms are well informed on beginning pumping if baby is born early and not feeding well, or any reason a bottle is being given after or in place of breastfeeding. 

Triple feeding means that you do three things every time you feed your baby – nurse, bottle feed, and pump. The idea is that first you nurse your baby as much as you can, then, if your baby is still hungry or not feeding well, you top them off with a bottle of either pumped breast milk or formula. Then, to make sure your supply stays even with what your baby is taking, you pump in order to remove as much milk as possible.

The hope is the triple feeding plan is temporary until baby is feeding better, but sometimes there is indication to have to do this plan longer if concern on milk supply or baby’s feedings. With mom’s mental health being priority, it is very important this plan is done in under one hour so mom has time to rest and take care of herself between feedings. Having your partner to help with bottle feeding while pumping is very helpful.  I also encourage moms to take a break from the plan occasionally and solely pump and bottle feed as needed. 

Breastfeeding babies who come early can be complicated and concerning to meeting your breastfeeding goals. The biggest thing to remember is if there is reason to give baby a supplement, make sure to pump & protect your milk supply!

Too many times, I have met disappointed women with low milk supply who were never informed how to remove milk from their breasts in a way to build and maintain supply.

The best way, of course is the feed the baby at the breast on demand from birth. But sometimes things happen that interrupt that- and many times a dyad who leaves the hospital supplementing (feeding the baby by any method other than only at the breast) will need to give their breasts extra stimulation to make the milk to meet their baby’s demands. 

These women may not own a pump, they may not know how to hand express or they may have the latest double electric pump and be using it inefficiently.💔 

In order to keep making milk, the breasts need to have milk removed from them FREQUENTLY. If the baby is not feeding effectively or if your baby isn’t latching, you should be mimicking what a newborn normally does- which is drain the breast up to 14ish times a day. 8 times is the minimum you should be removing milk from your breasts.

Studies show most women get the bulk of the milk out in a 10 min pump. There is no need to pump for 20 or 30 min- this is just tiring you out!

In the beginning you may not see much milk. Keep going! Breast stimulation is needed to make milk.

The overnight emptying of the breasts is a strong driver of prolactin levels. Prolactin is the hormone that we need for milk production. Prolactin peaks in the night. So even though you want to sleep, waking to feed the baby or pump overnight at least once will help you make more milk! Pump around the clock!

The frequency of pumping for exclusively pumping moms can be different from mom to mom once their milk supply is established. 

See an IBCLC!

After struggling with PCOS and weight gain for many years, Alleigh took the step of having gastric bypass surgery and successfully lost 100 lbs. Proud to be what she called “the healthiest I’ve ever been,” Alleigh was excited to try for a baby. She quickly got pregnant and everything was going well.

Alleigh planned for a natural birth; however, she ended up experiencing several birth complications. Once discharged, Alleigh soon recognized signs of hunger in her newborn, even though he was nursing very frequently. “My nipples were torn up and he wasn't having hardly any wet and dirty diapers,” she remembers. “He had his first doctor appointment at five days old and he had lost just under a pound. I was told to see a lactation consultant and start triple feeding. I cried and cried and cried. I felt worthless. Useless. I felt like a terrible mother.”

She began using an SNS and battled through postpartum depression before finding support in the IGT and Low Milk Supply Group on Facebook, which also began to help her connect the dots on how her health history might have impacted her ability to make milk. She also found what worked for her in terms of continuing her nursing relationship with her son. “I have come to terms with my low milk supply and we exclusively nurse with a DIY SNS,” she says. “I'm an advocate for low milk supply. Although we don’t “manage” FPIES- this is absolutely done by an allergist- we DO support families with FPIES. 

Even if there is only one trigger food, understandably families can be really anxious about feeding their little one or about accidental exposures outside of their care. They can struggle to meet their little one’s nutrition needs depending on the trigger food. 

The main time we see FPIES is with families who are also struggling with other food allergies or intolerances (like CMPA). Some families are having to avoid upwards of 5 foods because of food allergies/intolerances and FPIES. We have also supported families that have needed to eliminate many many more than 5 foods and by the time we see them, feeding their kids is stressful and a full time job.

When we work with these families we:
-Assess their little one’s diet to ensure they are getting what they need to THRIVE
-If there are any gaps we find ways to tackle this through foods that won’t cause a reaction 
-support families to have plans in place for care outside of the home (I.e childcare and with grandparents)
-Liaise with GPs, paediatricians an allergist if blood tests are needed because we have identified gaps that may need supplementation 
-Support parents to continue breastfeeding on an elimination diet if needed
-Support families with recipes, product recommendations and ideas to make feeding their families easier and less stressful so their mental and physical energy isn’t as consumed with food. 

It is honestly a huge privilege to be able to do this and we feel so lucky to have helped so many families.

Many nursing parents have questions about supplementation. One method is by finishing at the breast.

Breastfeeding 35 to 38 week gestation babies 
Dropping top ups gradually 

So your baby is around full term, starting to wake themselves for feeds, more alert and beginning to feed more effectively. So how do we go about moving away from topping up?

Disclaimer: when beginning to reduce topping up it is very important to keep a close eye on nappy output and weight gain and ideally be under the guidance of a breastfeeding counsellor or IBCLC

Make sure baby is coming to the breast every feed if possible

Encourage baby to have both breasts each feed before topping up Wake with a nappy change if necessary

If babies are having large volume top ups, 50-60ml or more, then it can be a good plan to reduce the volume first. Babies can be put back on the breast after the top up if necessary. They will trigger another let down of milk so baby can take more. Topping up mid feed like this works really well as it breaks the association of needing a bottle to settle

Once smaller volumes are working you can try to stop some of the top ups. Most find mornings are a good time. Parents often seem to have more milk in the mornings and babies tend to be more settled. Put baby back on the breast for another go if necessary. Night feeds can also be quite easy stop topping up as the babies begin to settle back to sleep after the lovely surge of oxytocin

Encourage natural cluster feeding behaviour. Babies often love to cluster feed in the evenings and this can actually be very useful  to increase breastfeeding as they are highly motivated to feed! Also anecdotally we have noticed on @bftwinsuk that there seems to be a period of frequent feeding around 40 week due date. So this is also useful for the same reason, babies suddenly WANT to breastfeed loads!

Things to remember: babies generally like to feed more frequently than 3 hourly, babies often like both breasts, babies should have at least 6 wet nappies and 2 poos a day up until 6 weeks, cluster feeding is normal newborn behaviour, babies do not like to be put down very much so try cuddling them if you need a break from feeding, or give baby to someone else to cuddle!

We love all babies, born at any gestational age.

But there are unique challenges that come when a baby is born early, around 36 or 37 weeks. 

These babies are known as “the great pretenders”; they LOOK like full term babies. But they ACT very much like preemies.

All of the typical guidance you hear like “never wake a sleeping baby”, or “follow the baby’s cues and feed on demand” won’t really work to keep these babies growing. 

These babies are tough, because they are:
1. Sleepy. They won’t always wake on their own to eat, and the often fall asleep soon into a breastfeeding session.
2. Not strong- in fact sometimes babies born just sightly early will not be very effective at drawing milk out of the breast or even the bottle.
3. Not feisty- if given a pacifier sometimes these little ones will happily suck on a paci and skip a meal altogether, whereas an older baby would spit out the paci and protest for milk.

If you’ve had a late preterm baby, you get it. If you’ve worked with these babies (hello fellow L&D nurses! Hello fellow lactation consultants!), you get it. 

It’s HARD work to get these babies fed and keep them growing, but about 1 week after their due date you’ll see a very different baby. You just gotta keep going, and get evidence-based help on your side.

Before I gave birth I just figured I’d breastfeed. I didn’t really think about it much, I just thought if I could I would, simple as that. Easy peasy. I also never thought I’d ever share a breastfeeding picture, but no one talks about breastfeeding. Everyone talks about pregnancy and birth, but not this part and it deserves more attention and support. Moms are asked if they “plan” to breastfeed. And then when they say yes they get no education or support regarding it, especially after leaving the hospital which is crazy because of all my mom friends, none of them have had a flawless breastfeeding journey. 

LOL breastfeeding is FAR from easy. 

Triple feeding was my life for 6.5 weeks. Try to nurse, then pump every 2-3 hours, then bottle feeding what you pumped. Waking at 2am trying to nurse and then pumping and feeding, and again at 5am and all day every day wondering why you’re doing what you’re doing. Why you don’t just stop and give your baby formula if it’s really this hard? Tracking every ounce and minute they nurse and every dirty and wet diaper. Weighing your baby obsessively to make sure they’re gaining. 

Having your baby kick and scream and cry when you try to nurse them is the worst form of rejection. 

Tears, SO MANY tears. 

Wanting to give up, reaching out to all your mom friends so they can tell you not to give up but it’s okay to take a break. Feeding your baby is essential, it doesn’t matter how you do it, you’re still an amazing mama. I knew this and I believe this, it’s just not what I wanted and I’m pretty stubborn.

I didn’t give up. We kept trying. It took 6 weeks that felt like absolute hell and a revision of tongue and lip ties by a skilled pediatric dentist after our pediatrician told us she didn’t have them. But we are now successfully breastfeeding and it is one of my biggest accomplishments and something I’m so proud of. 

For me it was a dream to be able to feed my baby breast milk no matter how long I did or how she got it. 

I hope all mamas, nursing or pumping or formula feeding know how amazing they are. 💕 I hope all mamas never think they “quit” or “failed.” Every journey is special. 💜
