Who has heard of triple feeding? 

Triple feeding is a process of feeding a newborn that requires 3 steps every feed. 
1 - Breastfeeding 
2 - Pumping 
3 - Bottle Feeding (pumped breast milk typically) 

This is often done when babies have a hard time breastfeeding for a variety of reasons such as prematurity, tongue ties, and medical issues. All in the hopes of keeping up weight gain and eventually exclusively breastfeeding. 

This has been our reality again for the last 3 weeks. It’s tough. But it’s not forever. Triple feeding has a means to an end, or it should anyways. 

One important thing with triple feeding is it can wear your out so it’s important to protect your sanity as well. If this is a path you are put on always know that you can stop, you don’t have to continue. And fed is best. Whether that’s with formula, pumped breast milk or by breastfeeding. Don’t ever let anyone persuade you into continuing to pump or triple feed if it’s affecting your mental health, only do it if you want to. 

For us we do pumped breast milk through a Supplemental Nursing System (SNS) or also known as tube at breast, rather than a bottle at this time.

Have you ever wondered if your baby is burning too many calories by breastfeeding or chestfeeding? Maybe you were told to limit time at the breast/chest in order to keep them from losing too much weight?

Well, according to a study done in preterm infants (over 32 weeks gestation), babies burn the same amount of calories feeding from a breast/chest as a bottle despite feeding longer at the breast/chest!

The study was small, but the results are great! Infants can safely feed for longer periods at the breast/chest and not burn extra calories.

The only time I suggest limiting time at the breast/chest is for maternal mental health. If baby nurses for 45 minutes and then you are pumping and supplementing, decreasing that time at the breast/chest so your overall feeding schedule isn’t 1.5 hours and you have to repeat it again in an hour is helpful!

Whether it’s 3, 5, or 10% of the population, there are people that struggle to or never make a full milk supply. From 1 month to 1 year, exclusively breastfed babies average 25oz of breast milk per day. True low supply means making less than this when the breasts are stimulated every 1-3 hours day and night. Chronic low milk supply is linked to either a greater health concern or something out of your control which you cannot change or fix with cookies, teas or even sometimes medications and pumping. 

🗝Low milk supply that can be increased with time and support:
💡Baby not feeding efficiently from lack of oral motor skill or tongue tie
💡Taking certain prescription medications with a side effect of dropping milk (Sudafed, Benadryl, antibiotics)
💡Not feeding or pumping enough, especially over night
💡Scheduled feedings or over use of a pacifier
💡Birth. Many medications designed to help you labor and deliver actually inhibit baby from latching and feeding effectively for hours to days after birth. Hemorrhage or birth trauma can also cause low supply in the beginning
💡Supplementing, especially in the two weeks after birth 

🗝Reasons for chronic low milk supply that may not increase even with maximal support:
💡Insufficient glandular tissue (IGT). Breasts never developed during puberty and look tubular or widely spaced. Signs of IGT include breasts did not grow in puberty, or increase in size during pregnancy. No engorgement in the week after birth
💡Uncontrolled or undiagnosed thyroid disorder
💡Uncontrolled diabetes
💡Hormone or endocrine disorders, including severe PCOS
💡Hormonal birth control placed/used too soon after delivery 
💡Breast or nipple surgery, augmentation, reduction, trauma
💡Nipple piercing that scars shut instead of staying open

There is a mistaken belief that prescription galactagogues, teas, or herbs can cure ANY chronic low milk supply. Before self-prescribing or taking Domperidone, Reglan, fenugreek, or any other lactation supplement, consider having your serum prolactin levels tested and a full evaluation by a skilled lactation consultant. Continue to follow @lalactation for strategies of breastfeeding with chronic low milk supply.

Our breastfeeding journey was the opposite of what I envisioned and that was devastating. 

I was told on day 4 that our issues were because I had low supply - but when I later brought up concerns that Mari would gag and choke while nursing, I was then told that I had a fast letdown…it didn’t really make sense to me that someone could have both but as a first time mom, I assumed the medical and health professionals knew what they were talking about. 

And when I had 3 days of nonstop breast pain due to clogged ducts week 2, I was told my body was just adjusting. 

I will never know this for sure, but I believe that my supply was actually fine initially - but Mari’s inability to latch and effectively extract milk meant that it wasn’t being removed. As a result of this, my body stopped producing early on. 

By week 3, I had shifted to nursing Mari only once a day trying to give my nipples a break. I pumped for multiple sessions, both breasts, and would get about this…less than half an ounce. 

I learned a LOT about pumping and will share what worked for me for sure but THIS image feels important. I remember tapping the side of the bottles to get every single drop and how big and deep my feelings of inadequacy were because I wasn’t producing for my baby. I saw no images of breastmilk production where bottles weren’t full…so to anyone who might be struggling and putting this out, or who looks at this and hopes “one day”…you’re not alone. 

Also, to anyone out there who is pregnant or breastfeeding and can, do yourself and your little love a favor and find an incredible lactation consultant immediately.

We're done being dismissed by our providers. We're done accepting the myth that breastfeeding has to be all or nothing, and the myth that true low supply doesn't exist.

WE. DESERVE. BETTER.

Chronic low milk supply is NOT in your head. 
It is NOT your fault. 
Your body has NOT simply “failed.” 

Rather, parents who suffer from chronic low milk supply have been failed by the false dogma that suggests lactation is a naturally “perfect” process, and a medical establishment that consistently diminishes and dismisses women’s health concerns.

The bottom line: in the absence of breast surgery or mismanagement, chronic low milk supply is a red flag for a hormonal, structural and/or anatomical issue with the lactating parent, the infant, or both. There are things you can do to investigate the possible root cause(s) as well as to have a better breastfeeding experience. And just as with any chronic health condition, you deserve support, validation and answers – even if the problem can’t be fixed. Because #everydropcounts.

“Bring baby it breast for each feed and then when they are finished, offer some formula to top them off.”

Have you heard this before?

Many well-intentioned health care providers give this advice, particularly if the baby is slow to gain weight, is still working on learning how to latch, or “until milk comes in.” Although there are times when formula is medically indicated in babies, there is a key piece of information that many people do not include in their advice.

What can happen is that babies get some breastmilk from feeding directly, and then take formula when offered. This can lead to babies feeling more full than they otherwise would have, which can lead to less frequent feeding at the breast or a less vigorous suck at the next feed.

So when the next feed comes around, baby may not remove as much milk. Parents worry because it was a short feed and offer formula again, which the baby often takes. This cycle continues and the baby may feed less and less at the breast, which can ultimately lead to a decline in milk production, which further perpetuates less feeding at the breast and more from the bottle.

So what to do if your baby is not feeding effectively at the breast? Bring them to breast, pump, and then give the pumped milk. If there is not enough milk to give, THEN give formula when indicated. The key is to pump every time that formula is give, so that your body gets the stimulation it needs to keep making milk!

Triple feeding is when you are breastfeeding your baby plus pumping and then topping up your baby with a bottle of either expressed milk or formula.

Triple feeding is exhausting and really hard work. Most families end up triple feeding because there are concerns about their babies weight gain, low supply, late preterm or early term babies who aren't able to feed well at the breast or babies with an underlying medical issue.

Babies who are triple fed will often breastfeed then have a bottle and the breastfeeding parent pumps after feeds. When I am working with families I often advise them to give the bottle first and finish on the breast. This maintains a positive association for the baby with the breast. This is really important to prevent breast refusal.

Triple feeding is a short term solution and not something that you should be doing for weeks and weeks. If you are triple feeding you need a thorough plan which has definitive timeline including moving away from triple feeding. 

It is not something people can sustain long term. If you're triple feeding you should work with an IBCLC.

Triple feeding, der involverer amning, pumpning og supplering med udmalket mælk eller modermælkserstatning, kan være en belastning for både mor og baby. Selvom det kan være nødvendigt i visse tilfælde, er det vigtigt at forstå de udfordringer, det kan medføre. Husk at overveje, hvad der er bedst i jeres situation.

baby. Det er afgørende at få god støtte og vejledning, hvis du oplever problemer med amningen. 

Husk, at hvile også er essentielt for en vellykket ammeopstart. Sørg for at få hvile og pas godt på dig selv, så du kan være der for din baby. Brug dit netværk ❤️

Sunde og raske børn født til termin klarer sig ofte bedst ved friamning - amning efter behov. Jo mere du ammer, jo før løber mælken til og jo mere mælk har du. 
Friamning betyder, at baby skal have brystet, når det viser tegn på sult, og ikke nødvendigvis følge en stram tidsplan. Det er vigtigt at amme efter barnets behov og ikke vente på der er gået 3 timer. 

Ved at lytte til din babys behov og din egen krop, kan du skabe en mere afslappet og rar ammeoplevelse.

Triple Feeding, is when mums are offering breastfeeds, pumping and bottle feeding for topups. Usually a temporary process to help increase the mums supply whilst increasing or protecting a babies weight

For anyone in this cycle, they will agree that it is exhausting and feels difficult to maintain the commitment it requires due to the length of time each feed takes 

So how can we make it more sustainable? By reducing the time it involves! 

🤱Keep the feeds efficient, no sleeping babies until the end of the feed! 
⛽️Use a good, strong breastpump that allows for double pumping (ensuring use of correct flange size!) 
🍼Have bottles clean and ready to go! Infant formula can actually be prepared in advance safely! 
Breastmilk can even safely be given cold ( just the babies are often fussy and like it warm!) 

Lactation consultants can guide and tweak the triple feeding schedule to ensure your commitment is maintained

For those in this cycle, hang in there! And for those who have been through it please share some words of encouragement in the comments

No matter the circumstance or root cause(s), when you are focused on #exclusivelybreastfeeding (aka #nursing only) and you struggle with #lowsupply, it can feel devastating.

I know that when I was going through this I would not have listened to this statement - in fact, my husband told me something along these lines countless times - and it didn’t matter. But YOUR WORTH AS A MOTHER IS NOT DEFINED BY THE OUNCES YOU PRODUCE!

For anyone who did or who is currently struggling with anything close to this, whether it is supply issues or the decision that nursing is just not for you, please read this over and over and over again. Say it out loud. Print it and tape it all around your house as a reminder - do whatever you need to do to remind yourself of this often.

I used to be one of those people. Who thought low supply only happened to <1% of moms. 

For reasons we don’t fully understand yet, the percentage of moms who can’t produce enough to feed their babies is rising, and may be as much as 15%. 

Could it be rising hormonal issues like PCOS or other medications moms take for fertility or diabetes? More moms with thyroid disease? It’s hard to say but I feel for any mama who has been invalidated by a lactation professional saying that it’s impossible for her to not make enough milk. 

And just because your low supply is caused by ‘secondary’ problems (breastfeeding mismanagement, birth trauma, your need for sleep) doesn’t mean it’s *your* fault. That is 100% a failure of the system and lack of support. 

That’s why I want to empower all moms when it comes to their breastfeeding goals. I highly recommend the book Making More Milk by Diana West, IBCLC.

I also have a free guide at the link in my bio to get on top of problems and learn how to tune into your baby’s innate instincts to breastfeed from birth ✨🤍✨

Many families are discharged from hospital breastfeeding and topping up. Many families are being advised to top up in the first couple of weeks due to feeding/weight issues. Many families are then not supported to drop these top-ups once baby is stronger, more alert and feeding better. 
One of my most read articles is "Dropping top ups gradually" which you can find here https://kathrynstaggibclc.com/2018/01/26/dropping-top-ups-gradually/

Here is an overview.

I must stress that you need to make sure baby is feeding well before you start this process, and keep a close eye on nappy output and weight gain.

This process can be done without pumping, but will be quicker if you can manage to pump as well.

STAGE 1
*Feed frequently. Breastfeed at the earliest feeding cue. Wake baby if it is coming up to 3 hours from the start of the last feed and they are still asleep. The MINIMUM a baby should be fed is 8 times in 24 hours. Most babies like to feed more frequently once they are more alert.
*Ensure baby is going to the breast every feed. Especially at night when prolactin levels are at their highest. If you miss a feed, pump!
*Offer the second breast. Once the "active feeding" stage (see "what a breastfeed should look like") is finished and baby is just comfort sucking, or baby has come off or gone to sleep, wake baby, perhaps with a nappy change, and offer the second breast. Baby should actively feed again due to faster flowing milk.
*Give top up.
*Pump when you can.

STAGE 2
*Continue to offer both breasts.
*Reduce volume of top ups.
*Put baby back on the breast if not settled after the smaller top up. This will stimulate another let down of milk and boost your supply.
*Pump when you can.

STAGE 3
*Stop one or two top ups completely. Choose a time of day (often mornings) when baby generally feeds well and just put them back on the breast with no top up, several times if necessary. This cluster feeding will help boost your supply.
*Continue to breastfeed and top up as normal the rest of the day.
*Pump when you can.

STAGE 4
*Aim to top up half the breastfeeds.
*Then drop one top up at a time until you are no longer having to top up at all.
*Gradually reduce pumping.

It’s not uncommon for parents to be told by a health care professional that their newborn needs supplementing with formula, or for nursing mothers to give formula because they are worried their baby is not getting enough from the breast. This might sometimes be the case, but unfortunately, it is not uncommon for babies to be given formula supplementation unnecessarily.

If you have given your baby formula, please don’t think this will spell the end of your breastfeeding journey. I have worked with dozens of parents who have supplemented with formula, sometimes when it was needed, and sometimes when it wasn't, and who have gone on to breastfeed very successfully. I’ve recently written a detailed article about how to protect your breastfeeding journey if your baby is receiving supplemental feeds, which is in ‘My Resources’ on my website (see link in bio). 

If a mother is producing significantly less milk than her baby needs, she is unlikely to be able to substantially increase her supply solely by breastfeeding. This is because once the flow of milk in the breast slows down, babies no longer have the incentive to drink deeply, and will either move to non-nutritive sucking or will simply refuse to stay on the breast. But pumps will suck and stimulate production whether there is milk in the breast or not.

Therefore, when giving formula top ups, in order to move to exclusive breastfeeding, most women will need to spend some time ‘triple feeding’, which entails:

-  Breastfeeding

-  Double pumping shortly after breastfeeds

-  Giving top ups (which can happen before or after pumping)

As your supply increases thanks to the pumping, there is a good chance you will be able to replace the formula with more and more of your own milk. Once all the milk your baby is drinking via the bottle is your breastmilk, then you can slowly reduce the top ups and pumping and move to exclusive breastfeeding. #breastfeeding #responsivefeeding #expressingmilk #pumpingmilk #ardopumps #triplefeeding

If you have not heard of triple feeds, it’s when the nursing parent ends up triple feeding when their baby isn’t gaining sufficient weight via nursing.

Milk donation is over. 

After 5 months, I am no longer going to donate milk. My baby is still exclusively breastfed (yay!) and I am not over-producing enough to meet the Danish minimum for donating anymore (200 mL/day). My current overproduction is around 150 mL/day and it will go towards building a stash for when my baby goes to the nursery. 

I feel strangely sad about it. It wasn't my plan to donate. I just wanted to breastfeed my own baby. But he was born premature, and was unable to feed himself at first. So I had to pump, and literally endured three whole weeks of triple feeding in order to build up my supply and feed him with pumped milk. 

He had 2 days of pumped milk + supplement, and then only had breast milk. We fed him with the syringe for 3 weeks, and then he transitioned to pumped milk in a bottle, and then we slowly increased the amount of milk he would get at the breast. At 7 weeks he finally didn't need pumped milk anymore. 

I had surplus from the 3rd day onwards and started donating as early as legally possible in Denmark (baby had to be one month old to start the screening process). At that stage I already had 3.7 liters stashed in my deep freezer and ready to be donated. Then I consistently donated around 2 liters every week, until my surplus started to dwindle in December. 

Triple feeding is absolutely brutal. Doing it for 3 weeks was a major feat.  Being able to breastfeed a preemie with feeding issues has been a struggle, and I am very proud for being able to do it. Donating so much milk on the side is another victory, even if it wasn't part of my initial plan. 

Goodbye donor 27! 

Thank you @medela_scandinavia for saving my milk supply. It wouldn't have been possible to breastfeed without a very good pump.

Part 1 | My Breastfeeding Journey

I felt inspired to share my breastfeeding journey by  @lutz.lactation & more importantly our struggles with breastfeeding. It has helped me to know that I am not alone on this journey, that others have faced the same challenges & overcame them with the right support & education. This is also a little bit of a health history of my sons first couple weeks of life, as his situation led us to a unique breastfeeding experience.

My sweet baby boy Hopi was born a little early at 37+1 due to me having several dangerous blood sugar drops from 34 weeks on, so he was considered “late pre-term” and quickly developed a bad case of jaundice. He was born with a bit of a recessed bottom jaw, I have very flat nipples, he was hypoglycemic at birth & had a very shallow latch. He was too weak and tired to latch at our first attempt so he received glucose gel & my delivery nurse promptly helped me hand express several drops of colostrum into a syringe. I was honestly mind blown that there was even colostrum in there [more on this another time]

We continued to work at latching throughout the night & I accepted help from anyone that wanted to offer. My nurses were so supportive & amazing at offering suggestions until I could meet with a lactation consultant the next day.

Over the course of our stay I met with several LC’s & they all assured me that with time Hopi would get stronger, be able to open his mouth wider, become more interested AND effective at nursing. I am so thankful to each LC I have worked with, their knowledge & hands on skills were so helpful on our journey.

The first 24 hours I tried to get him to latch any time he showed a hunger cue & we did tons of skin to skin. I was advised to pump for 15min. after every nursing session to help bring in my mature milk [I was never told that it would/could take a week+ to come in with me being diabetic].

Did you know we have different breast pump shell sizes available from the infant feeding team when you borrow one of our breast pumps? A nipple gauge is available to help you get the closest fit. Usually the size that fits closest to the nipple enables more effective expression, you might need a different size on each breast as breasts and nipples are unlikely to be exactly the same shape and size. Not all standard pump sizes are a close enough fit so smaller inserts are now available from the pump manufacturer that we use and inserts compatible with some shells are available to buy from other companies. It’s really important that the fit is comfortable as breast pumps can cause nipple pain and soreness just like an ineffective latch can. Last year we watched a brilliant lecture from @goldlactacademy on the difference a good flange fit can make by Jeanette Mesite Frem MHS, IBCLC, RLC, CCE who shared The Flange FITS™ Guide from her website http://babiesincommon.com . Part 3 | Breastfeeding journey 

Upon arrival to the ED
I had a breakdown. I didn’t know what to say when they asked why we were there, all I could do was cry & say something was wrong with my baby. I told them he was 5 days old & would not swallow/drink anything. They did all the normal admission things like temp, weight, BP, etc & I didn’t notice any of the numbers, but I noticed my baby was barely crying. None of it made him upset & I knew it should.

He was taken back to a room & right away the doctor on the floor came in. She attempted to give him his bottle & confirmed I did the right thing by bringing him when I did. Immediately they began treatment for jaundice, hypothermia, dehydration & an unstable heart rate. We were quickly transferred to a larger Pediatric hospital out of town & after 12 heartbreaking hours he had a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis. I had unknowingly become GBS+ at delivery.

He was so sick that he could not swallow or take anything by mouth. He received a continuous IV of saline & dextrose to give him nutrition along with an array of antibiotics until he was healthy enough to take a bottle. I continued to pump, but now I worried that the stress would delay my mature milk even further.

Finally, on day 7 of life he was able to take a bottle again. Two full days from my last attempt at bottle feeding. Now we had a whole new set of obstacles with him being in an isolette & being covered in wires & tubes. The next day he was stable enough to come out of the isolette & we were able to do skin to skin & attempt breastfeeding again. 

Breastfeeding was super challenging with all the cords hooked up to him & he was still pretty weak but we would try every 2-3 hours & follow up with a bottle of pumped milk & then formula if he needed more. We triple fed for the next 2 weeks while he continued antibiotics for the meningitis. It was so exhausting triple feeding, but he was finally gaining weight & was able to remove the IV nutrition.

It was exhausting. I was putting too much pressure on myself because I was nervous I would “fail”, that it was my fault she had been marked failure to thrive. Scared she’d get sick without my antibodies to protect her.
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
I remember feeling proud of this bottle of milk. I spent all day collecting it. It was the first and one of the only bottles full of my breast milk that I gave her. 
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
It took several friends and my IBCLC to help me realize that my worth as a mom isn’t defined by the amount of breast milk I create. That it was okay to feed my baby both breast milk and formula without “failing”. It took several professionals to help me realize that Ophelia had several restrictions preventing her from latching and sucking correctly. It took more research to help me understand how hormonal disorders can affect milk supply. 
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
My point is, you and your baby’s feeding journey can look so many different ways. And whichever way works best for both of your overall mental and physical health, is the perfect way. For Ophelia and I, that looked like breastfeeding for a little bit, then bottle feeding formula. 
⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
And whatever way it looks like for you- be proud. Keeping a tiny human alive is NOT a small feat, but you are doing it, and you are doing it well.

One of the first signs that baby is getting enough breast milk is that mom is comfortable. If there isn’t any pain and mom is comfortable, that is a sign that baby is transferring milk from the breast.

All we have are our stories. This is a long one. But worth the read. ⠀⠀
The first year of Carson’s life was confusing. He was happy! But I remember feeling shame and defeated the entire first year. I would dread the doctor visits. In fact, sometimes I would cry on the way there because I knew he wouldn’t weigh enough. ⠀⠀
You see, the first week, he gained weight. Milk would literally shoot into his mouth and he was on track to gaining back his birth weight. I mean, I felt like I could maybe do this mom thing!!! 💪🏻
⠀⠀
Then the second week came. And he had to actually remove the milk and he wasn’t. I would nurse for 20 minutes on each side. Thinking he was eating. Thinking all was well. Then we went to the checkup. And no weight gain. ⠀⠀
Triple feeding. That was the answer. Feed the baby for 40 minutes. Pump for 20. Feed for 20. Around the clock. It was in those dark moments in the middle of the night, I felt shame. That I couldn’t even feed my baby. What kind of mother can’t feed their baby?!? And I would tell myself the cruelest things. ⠀⠀
He still wouldn’t eat. Not really anyway. No tummy troubles. No reflux. Just not hungry. I quit the nursing. Went straight to pumping so we could know every ounce he ate. And we would write everything down. Rounding up because I wanted to end the day at 14-15 ounces. ⠀⠀
We did this his entire first year. After work I would pick him up from daycare and he would have ate 6 ounces all day. And I knew, there was no way I could make up the difference in a few hours. ⠀⠀
It consumed me. It’s how I measured if I was a good mom. I was a mess inside. Frantic for someone to tell me that he’s fine. Instead we would go to the doctor and she would confirm that I’m a terrible mother with the discussion of “failure to thrive.” ⠀⠀
When he was one, he weighed a little over 15 pounds. Was wearing 9 month clothes. And HAPPY! Just small. Yet I allowed them to do a series of tests. I held his helpless body down while they attempted to draw a large amount of blood from his tiny arm. And after what seemed like hours of both of us crying and multiple failed attempts, I said NO MORE! ⠀⠀
Trust your gut. Empower yourself. You are enough.

My husband and I chatted leading up to the delivery of our fourth baby. I let him know my feelings and "plan" (quotation because if there is one thing I have learned in my years of parenting, it's that sometimes, many times, things won't go according to plan and we'll need to pivot). I let my husband know what I wanted, we discussed my limits & needs, and we prepared by purchasing things I knew I would need. 

Things we bought: 
- New Nipple shields, we purchased extra so there would always be an emergency set in the diaper bag & our vehicle (I have inverted nipples and even with expression they didn't evert enough for baby to latch). 

- New & extra sets of pump parts. Another big factor when you have inverted nipples is having the right size pump parts. This was something no one really told me until I had our third and the most wonderful God sent angle lactation consultant (that I also had the honor of working with) taught me SO much and changed everything for us. She was the first to ever get my milk moving and baby feeding. [This deserves a WHOLE post, so I'll share about that another day].

- New pump. I spent the whole pregnancy researching every pump under the sun. I ultimately decided to give the Spectra a try and spent my time showering the internet to get my hands on one in Canada. It wasn't easy, but after having tried almost every pump available only he Canadian market, and given my specific needs for a large flange size not offered by all companies, it was our best shot at success. I ended up being able to secure not one, but two brand new pumps. Yay! I set myself up for success with ensuring I had multiple sets of flanges, extra pump parts & adaptors (I used a 'hack' to be able to use the spectra pump with my medela mamymom flanges - as these are the only flanges that come in my size). 

My plan was simple - we would give it another shot and if it wasn't working, we wouldn't force it. We wouldn't go down without a fight, but we would give it our best shot and not get upset if things didn't work out again.

Let’s talk about Pros and cons to exclusive breastfeeding. ⁣

⁣

⁣
⁣
𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬: ⁣
⁣

⁣

⁣
✨ Even though bonding was amazing it was tiring when he preferred me.⁣
⁣
✨ No control over my body, gained weight. ⁣
⁣

We’ve been there!
*It is really hard!*
Breast-feeding, bottlefeeding, and pumping all at once, around the clock, on top of everything else – is very difficult. Give yourself a break! Ask for help and take care of yourself too.

*It isn’t sustainable.*
The amount of time and energy it takes to triple feed is huge and moms end up stressed, exhausted and oftentimes, miserable. Their risk for perinatal mood and anxiety issues increases dramatically. It isn't a long term solution for a feeding problem.

*You need an end date.*
Setting an end date can help you manage the stress of triple-feeding. It will give you time to consider alternative feeding options and come up with a longer term solution that will work for you and your baby. 

*Your needs are important too*
While breastmilk is wonderful, feeding your baby shouldn't come at the expense of your own mental health. There are many ways for babies to be fed and for moms to rest and be able to enjoy other aspects of their baby. If you are struggling with feeding, find a local feeding consultant who can help and support you in your feeding relationship, no matter what that looks like. Remember, a happy mom = a happy baby.

Infant formula is not a sterile product, and it can become contaminated during the manufacturing process and during its time in the home environment. 

I find parents are often unaware of this method of preparation and also don't know that preparing in advance is possible. I recommend preparing in advance as this reduces the steps often involved in the feeding process if a baby is having breastfeeds, breastmilk and some infant formula. 

Please note, as an IBCLC I cannot recommend a specific formula although I get this question all the time!

Breastfeeding Bandaids can be needed, but should always be a short term solution while the root cause of the issue is figured out.⁠ Bandaids can help symptoms but not solve problems. 
⁠
🔶NIPPLE SHIELDS:⁠
Nipple shields are often used when a baby can't latch or when there is pain with latching.  Neither situation is normal and the cause should be figured out in order to make a plan to get off the nipple shield.⁠
⁠
🔶PUMPING AFTER BREASTFEEDS⁠
Sometimes parents pump after feeds at the breast in order to increase supply so the baby has more easy milk.  Again, this can be effective short term, but the baby should be able to maintain milk supply on his own and often there are simple solutions to help baby do this and decrease that workload for mama.⁠
⁠
🔶TRIPLE FEEDING⁠
Triple feeding is when you feed at the breast, pump and then feed that milk back either via bottle, finger feeding, cup feeding etc.  Triple feeding, like other bandaids, can be needed short term.  However, it is too much work to be a long term solution. ⁠
⁠
🔶REFLUX MEDS⁠
True acid reflux in babies is rare and usually only seen in preterm babies.  More commonly I see reflux due to swallowing air either because of a bad latch or because of an uncoordinated swallow OR reflux due to a food sensitivity.  Either way reflux meds are a bandaid to cover up why it is happening and this bandaid is not benign.  These meds were never studied on babies for safety, but retrospective research has shown that when given as a baby, they increase the baby's chances of broken bones as a child.⁠
⁠
🔶NIPPLE CREAM⁠
There are some great and not so great nipple creams out there for damaged nipples, but either way, they shouldn't be relied upon long term to keep pain or damage at bay. 
⁠
If you are using a bandaid and want to stop, find someone that is willing to dig in the weeds with you and figure out the root cause and also a way to fix that root cause!⁠
⁠

From a webinar from @United States Lactation Consultant Association about this concept to add a pump while baby is breastfeeding, in the early days to help get baby maximum milk intake.

Because breasts work in tandem with their letdowns (great for twins when you are tandem feeding) you can both capture a let down on the pump side, and also encourage let down on the baby's side. Double win right there.

The extra milk can be used to supplement a sleepy or jaundiced new baby after the feed, saved for the next feeding if a supplement is needed, or stored for later use. 

Many families ask me when they can start pumping, and especially those who are going back to work as they are feeling the pressure to start collecting milk. 

🌟If breastfeeding is going well, you can start pumping anytime.🌟
 
If it is not going well, you will likely need to start pumping right away.

 So it pays to have a pump that you can easily use that works well for you.

I just loved this concept because it doesn't interfere with breastfeeding, but it gives parents that option of capturing lost milk that leaks on the other side, utilizes both breasts at each feeding (even if baby will only take one) and it has numerous applications for babies who need supplements, such as triple feeding which can be so exhausting and overwhelming for everyone in the family.

For this approach you can use any electric pump, a hand pump, or even a silicone pump like a Haakaa. 
(Note that if baby can efficiently remove milk, both beasts should be offered and the pump used on the first side after baby is on the 2nd.)

Expressing and storing your milk can be a minefield of information and overwhelm.  
🤯
How long your milk can be left safely, and then consumed, will depend on the temperature it is stored at.  
🌡
I've summarised the information from NHS sources in the UK.  To make life easy people have been told they can store it 6 hours at room temperature, 6 days in the fridge and 6 months in the freezer. *The CDC in the United States say up to 12 months in the freezer is permissible, but we don't have that guidance here.  
🚰
Milk can be defrosted by placing it in the fridge or running it under warm water if you need it quickly.  Top tip, if you're not sure if, or how much expressed milk your baby will take, store it in smaller quantities e.g. 1-3 oz bags so if they don't use it, less goes to waste.  
🥛
Some people never express their milk, some choose to and some people have no option but to.  I'm here to support what works for you and your family.  Save for later or share with someone who needs it.

What is triple feeding?

Triple feeding is a feeding process whereby baby is fed at the breast, followed immediately by mum expressing breastmilk, then followed by baby being fed a bottle (either expressed breastmilk or formula). This is often repeated for every feed.

The aim of this feeding process is to increase mum's breastmilk supply and also help babies gain weight if they are underweight or have had slow weight gain.

This is only done in particular circumstances and is a very demanding process.

After 3 #lowmilksupply feeding journey’s, here’s what I’ve found to be the most, and least, helpful tools:

Things you can probably not worry about:

🤷🏻‍♀️Lactation snacks and teas. Some people do find them helpful- but lots of my clients, and myself, who have experienced chronic low supply find them to be a waste of time, money, and energy. Unless you enjoy making the snacks and drinking the teas, don’t worry about it.

🤷🏻‍♀️The same goes for supplements.  I have said EVERY time that I wouldn’t go down that slippery slope again, only to have 10+ supplements a week in. I have found a handful, maybe, to be slightly helpful- but otherwise most are not necessary. And medications that are often prescribed for low suppliers come with side effects, like depression and anxiety, which are already way too prevalent postpartum. Before you go down that route, assess risk vs. benefit. 

I’ll talk more about some of these things during my Baby Feeding Basics webinar tomorrow (link in bio to sign up!)

Things that can be SUPER helpful:

🦄Haakaa pump- use this during feeds to get milk without pumping, or as a pumping alternative! 

🦄Nursing AND pumping tank- two birds, one stone.

🦄Supplemental nursing system- I never loved mine, but I’ve heard that once you find a rhythm it can be helpful.

🦄Good quality pump with extra parts- if you choose to pump (you don’t have to) a good quality pump with extra parts is key.

🦄Positive combination feeding stories and support- if it makes you feel guilt or shame, walk away. Your mental health matters most.

🦄Someone to remind you that you aren’t a failure- over the years, I’ve found people who understood my journey and were there to remind me that I am not a failure and that my worth as a mother was so much more than how I fed my baby. Find you a someone like this. Shout out to my person @pathfinderdoulas

Today my breasts offer Hopi warm milk and fill his belly full, but even if they didn’t, I would still know they are worthy and play a vital role in nurturing his soul.

Triple Feeding is a treatment method used to increase supply in the breastfeeding person and to ensure adequate nutrition and weight gain in the infant. 
Triple feeding may become necessary when the baby is not transferring enough milk at the breast. This may be due to latching difficulties, insufficient breast stimulation, low milk supply or a medical reason such as prematurity. 

The goal is a temporary intervention as triple feeding is very demanding and exhausting for the breastfeeding parent and not sustainable long-term. 

It is called triple feeding because the breastfeeding person will do 3 things approx. every 3 hours.  
✅1.Direct breastfeeding 
✅2. Giving additional supplement (expressed milk, donor milk or formula). The required amount is individually different and should be elaborated in discussion with your health care professional based on evidence of intake at the breast, weight development and overall health status. 
✅3. Pumping both breasts, ideally with a hospital grade pump using techniques such as hands-on pumping to maximise milk output 

The main goals are: 
Feeding the baby enough milk so that they are gaining weight appropriately and have enough energy & strength to effectively feed from the breast 

Protect direct breastfeeding through increasing milk supply with additional stimulation typically from a hospital grade pump 

•And continuing to put the baby to the breast 

Depending on baby’s latch and medical condition, a supplemental nursing system should be considered for baby to receive the supplement at the breast. 
 
Ideally, the cycle of breastfeeding, pumping and supplementing shouldn’t last longer than 1 hour on average, so mum and baby can get some rest before the next feeding.If the baby is receiving the supplement through cup feeding or paced bottle feeding, it is helpful for the support person to feed the baby so that the breastfeeding person can focus on pumping.

Part 4 | Breastfeeding journey

We took Hopi home at 3 weeks old & continued triple feeding until he was 10 weeks. During those weeks there were times that he completely refused the breast. He would scream & arch his back until I gave him a bottle. When he did latch, it was still extremely painful for me & he would struggle to stay latched. It was like he was slipping or sliding off my nipple, and our nursing sessions were lasting for over an hour and he would be so upset when we were done nursing, almost like he was starving. As soon as he got a bottle he would be content & nap for an hour until we started the process over. 

I cried so many days & nights wanting breastfeeding to work, but I felt in my heart that something still wasn’t right with how it was going. My supply was horrible & I kept attributing it to me being diabetic, but I also felt he wasn’t transferring well since he was always so hungry after every nursing session. I was desperate for answers so I started researching anything & everything I could think of related to breastfeeding. Symptoms of oral ties kept popping up & we were both matched up for almost every. single. symptom 😭 

I researched heavily the process of having them revised & made an appointment with a pediatric dentist that specializes in oral ties. We went in for our consult & he was diagnosed with a severe lip tie & posterior tongue tie. [I don’t blame any of the LC’s that missed his ties, as many are not trained in oral ties & they are easily missed] [Also ties are more about oral function than just being tied, which he clearly had issues with] He had them laser revised that day & we had our first pain free breastfeeding session immediately after his procedure. It was the most beautiful thing & I cried tears of thanks.

**Postpartum Anxiety** (trigger warning)
I wish mammas would talk about postpartum anxiety. So today I'm opening up about my journey through it with both my children's births. No woman should suffer alone or feel like a bad mom because they can't snap out of it. We need each other and we need to normalize our journeys (even the rocky and rough ones).

While post partum mental health is talked about, it still seems to be a subject that gets skimmed over. Postpartum depression is usually the focus but I never once heard anyone I knew (or had doctors) talk about post partum anxiety. With my first I found myself blindsided days after bringing my sweet babe home with post partum anxiety and I didn't know what to do. I was sleep deprived, recovering from high blood pressure and a pretty traumatic birth, triple feeding, just trying to navigate how to get my baby to eat and on top of that (unbeknownst to me) had a partner dealing with anemia and was exhausted all the time no matter how many naps he had. It was a perfect storm.

Fast forward to my second baby (they are 15 months apart) and things looked a lot different. I still found myself hit hard with post partum anxiety the day I brought my baby home, but this time I had a plan in place that helped me through. 

I'm sharing over in my stories today all about what preplanning I had in place and the teams of people I asked to help me. This is the first time I'm sharing this but I plan on talking more about post partum anxiety in this space because I want to help other women be better prepared with tangible plans they can put in place. I wished someone had shared these same simple things with me when I had my first because it would have made a world of difference!

“Squeeze then swap” is usually my mantra for young babies with slow weight gain or sleepy at the breast or jaundiced and sleepy or needing top-ups and you’re triple feeding (breastfeeding, topping-up and expressing). 

The squeezing part means doing breast compressions to increase milk flow and therefore increase milk intake until you no longer notice frequent swallowing.

The swapping part means swapping sides once the swallows are not frequent even when doing the squeezing for a few minutes.

This can be continued many times during a feed until the baby is satisfied (hands relaxed, open and floppy) or a top-up if needed as the baby is still not frequently swallowing and is still hungry.

Putting a time on this is not helpful as mums and babies are unique.  Each person can have different amounts of milk ducts/capacity for carrying/making milk, different milk volumes at different times of the day and night, different milk flow, some fast and some slower and each baby can suck differently with more or less strength and coordination and latch differently due to many reasons. 

Babies respond to milk flow and so watching and responding to signs of actively drinking milk is much more helpful than watching the clock.

Dr Jack Newman has some great videos and information:

https://ibconline.ca/information-sheets/breast-compression/

Supply lines or supplemental nursing systems can work great in low supply situations when babies are latching well but needing top-ups.  Check out the great information on the ABA website:

https://www.breastfeeding.asn.au/bf-info/using-breastfeeding-supplementer

The most common is Cows Milk Protein Allergy (CMPA) or  Food Protein Induced Allergic Proctocolitis (FPIAP).

Awareness of non-IgE allergies is growing, allowing more parents to get the support they need. These allergies can be challenging to diagnose and manage, especially in young babies!

Symptoms may include blood or mucous in your babies stools, among others.

If non-IgE food allergies are suspected, a doctor may:

    •    Conduct tests to rule out other causes like infections or gastro issues.
    •    Recommend eliminating trigger foods from the breastfeeding mother’s or babies diet or change formulas. If symptoms improve, the food will later be reintroduced to confirm the diagnosis.

We had an awful night and the following afternoon the community midwife visited us, weighed her and discovered she had lost 13% of her birth weight. I knew I couldn't survive another 3 days with no sleep so I asked if I could go home and was told that would only be approved if my baby was getting milk (i.e. if I gave her formula as she wasn't able to latch to me despite me having loads of milk).

Whilst my eldest child may feel sad about not having the early start that she's seen me give her brother and sister, hopefully she will know that the passion and drive I have for my work is all for her.

Those silent, dark, *magnificent nights…

…when my body went into full warrior status at a time that I thought I was at my weakest.

…when I was so tired and depleted that I thought I was going to die when in reality I was so fully alive that I was living for two people, not just one.

Triple feeding means you breastfeed, then pump, and then bottle feed the pumped milk or formula and press repeat 8 to 10 times per day. 

While triple feeding takes lots of physical and emotional energy, there are some upsides, especially if your baby hasn't gained much weight or if your trying to get to the road of Exclusively breastfeeding!

Some reasons why we recommend triple feeding are:
Weight loss concerns for baby Jaundice concerns for baby 
Oral anatomy concerns
 (lip, tongue, buccal ties)
Goal is to exclusively breastfeed 
and plans to eagerly return to exclusive breast milk feeding once baby concern has been remedied.

Triple feeding has no specific timeline. Some women do it for a week and are able to re-establish supply and exclusively breastfeed. Some do it for months or throughout the duration of their breastfeeding journey. 
It works for some moms and not always for others. Triple feeding needs to be individualized to tailor your goals and your length of time. 
Usually, triple feeding is a short term solution. Which is why it’s so important to reach out for help from a lactation professional.

If you are triple feeding for an undetermined amount of time or for a short term goal, please seek help or different support!

We're done being dismissed by our providers. We're done accepting the myth that breastfeeding has to be all or nothing, and the myth that true and low supply doesn't exist.

WE. DESERVE. BETTER.

Chronic low milk supply is NOT in your head.
It is NOT your fault.
Your body has NOT simply “failed.”

Rather, parents who suffer from chronic low milk supply have been failed by the false dogma that suggests lactation is a naturally “perfect” process, and a medical establishment that consistently diminishes and dismisses women’s health concerns.

The bottom line: in the absence of breast surgery or mismanagement, chronic low milk supply is a red flag for a hormonal, structural and/or anatomical issue with the lactating parent, the infant, or both. There are things you can do to investigate the possible root cause(s) as well as to have a better breastfeeding experience. And just as with any chronic health condition, you deserve support, validation and answers – even if the problem can’t be fixed. Because #everydropcounts.

I felt unprepared as a new mom. Don’t get me wrong, I bought all the books and consumed a lot of advice, but I was full of doubt and worry that I would be good at this mom gig. I didn’t seem to have that intuition as a mom to know what to do when he cried. I struggled with nursing. The most fundamental thing we are supposed to be able to do: feed your baby. I couldn’t do it. I gave up after 3 weeks...

All because a scale told the doctors he wasn’t getting enough. So we switched to pumping and bottle feeds so we can monitor how much he was eating and I still couldn’t get him to consume more than 13-14 ounces a day. My life became consumed with his eating. I’d feel like a good mom if I was able to get him to eat the proper amount and a bad mom if I couldn’t. Which was 90% of the time.

When he was one we held him down screaming for blood draws and tests because he was still only 16 pounds and we had to rule out different things he might be sick with...just in case.

All because he was small. My gut told me he was healthy. God just made him little and he didn’t need a lot of food to grow and develop.

But I hadn’t learned to trust myself as a mom yet. I didn’t know what I didn’t know. All I know is after many failed attempts at getting a needle into his tiny arms for no real reason with tears running down my face I said no more. And I gathered up our things and I left that office, confused and angry.

I just spent his entire first year consumed with his eating and pooping and forgot to bask in the smiles and the laughter. I forgot to enjoy him growing up. I always had a dark shadow hanging over me. And I was desperate for change. It didn’t happen right away, but it’s the first time I knew that we as moms have to be empowered. We have to advocate for our children. Even if we aren’t as educated or have the credentials behind our names. Even then, we can have a voice. And our children are counting on us to use it.

A surprising amount of mamas start out with the wrong flange size when they first start pumping. Does pumping hurt? Do you have blanched nipples or a white or red ring at the base of the nipple after pumping? Are your nipples swollen after pumping? Your flanges may be either too small or too large, respectively. If this is you, check your pump manufacturer's website for proper sizing guidelines. Once you're in the correct size, adjust the suction to a place where you feel and see movement and a "tug," but no pain.  Not only will this be more comfortable, but you'll remove more milk!

Listened to a webinar from United States Lactation Consultant Association this weekend while prepping my upcoming CLE training, and came across this little gem. The concept is to add a pump while baby is breastfeeding, in the early days to help get baby maximum milk intake.
Because breasts work in tandem with their letdowns (great for twins when you are tandem feeding) you can both capture a let down on the pump side, and also encourage let down on the baby's side. Double win right there.
The extra milk can be used to supplement a sleepy or jaundiced new baby after the feed, saved for the next feeding if a supplement is needed, or stored for later use. 
Many families ask me when they can start pumping, and especially those who are going back to work as they are feeling the pressure to start collecting milk. If breastfeeding is going well, you can start pumping anytime. If it is not going well, you will likely need to start pumping right away. So it pays to have a pump that you can easily use that works well for you.
I just loved this concept because it doesn't interfere with breastfeeding, but it gives parents that option of capturing lost milk that leaks on the other side, utilizes both breasts at each feeding (even if baby will only take one) and it has numerous applications for babies who need supplements, such as triple feeding which can be so exhausting and overwhelming for everyone in the family.
For this approach you can use any electric pump, a hand pump, or even a silicone pump like a Haakaa.

Triple feeding means you breastfeed, then pump, and then bottle feed the pumped milk or formula and press repeat 8 to 10 times per day. 

While triple feeding takes lots of physical and emotional energy, there are some upsides, especially if your baby hasn’t gained much weight or if your trying to get to the road of Exclusively breastfeeding!

Some reasons why we recommend triple feeding are:
* Weight loss concerns for baby Jaundice concerns for baby 
* Oral anatomy concerns like tongue ties!
* Goal is to exclusively breastfeed 
and plans to eagerly return to exclusive breast milk feeding once baby concern has been remedied.

Triple feeding has no specific timeline. Some women do it for a week and are able to re-establish supply and exclusively breastfeed. Some do it for months or throughout the duration of their breastfeeding journey. 
It works for some moms and not always for others. Triple feeding needs to be individualized to tailor your goals and your length of time. 
Usually, triple feeding is a short term solution. Which is why it’s so important to reach out for help from a lactation professional.

✨TRIPLE FEEDING✨

Triple feeding is often prescribed by providers as the "solution" to issues such as slow weight gain, jaundice, poor latch, etc. It can be a great tool to help maintain nursing while resolving an issue, with the end goal being to have baby transferring milk successfully directly from the breast without supplementation. However, triple feeding is not usually sustainable long term. 

So what is triple feeding? It is where a mama will nurse baby as much as possible, then, provide baby with a bottle of either pumped breast milk or formula, and pump to signal the body that more milk was needed. This is to be done at EVERY feeding session while you are using this method.

These are my top 3 tips to make triple feeding suck less:
1. If possible, have someone else do the bottle feeding step so that you can focus on pumping.
2. If that is not a possibility, try to feed baby a bottle and pump at the same time to cut down on time (that next feeding can come quick- especially with triple feeding!)
3. Use a hands free pumping bra! Game changer!

TRIPLE FEEDING
 
It’s the tiresome task of breastfeeding, bottle feeding, and pumping to feed your baby. You might have been told to triple feed in order to protect your milk supply while your baby is supplemented by bottle. Maybe your baby has a difficult time latching and you can’t get enough food into your baby, so you’ve had to introduce bottle feeding. 

Whatever the case is, triple feeding is a tool used to support your baby to getting enough food while protecting your milk supply. It is NOT meant to be a long term solution. 

The support that parents need when triple feeding can be intensive and can be required for weeks. This is why I have made my Triple Feeding Support package 4 weeks in length. (and honestly, you get more than 4 weeks 😉) 

We first have to find out WHY you’re struggling with the issues you have and settle on the STRATEGIES you want to try. Sometimes these strategies take time. We also want to make sure you have a pump that is going to serve your needs for the short term intensive pumping that you have to do. This is why we set up a pump rental service – for those who just don’t have the resources to purchase an expensive pump with the kind of motor that can sustain frequent pumping.

Throughout our weeks together, we have check-in visits that allow you to pivot when you need to. Because if there’s one constant of newborn life, it is change! Things change from week to week and we are there to help you know when to pivot. 

Our ultimate goal is to help you bring your baby back to the breast. We want you to experience your own version of success – because success is different to everyone. There’s no “one-size-fits-all”.

#casestudy: A seven-day-old baby was brought to consult, as parents notice that she’s “constantly” looking for the breast. Mother wants to breastfeed exclusively and avoid formula as much as possible, but at the same time, she’s worried about starving her baby.

Baby did a good deep latch at our session, and nutritive sucking was observed for most of the time she was on the breast. However, I could only notice a few swallows. The pre and post weight-check revealed a milk transfer of less than an ounce. Clearly, something was going on here.

The oral examination showed a posterior tongue tie and a lip tie. Mom was pumping once a day and supplementing the baby with formula on every feeding after offering the breast. Thus, milk supply was low due to insufficient stimulation of the breast.

In this case, before I sent the family for a tongue tie evaluation, I decided to set them on triple feeding care.

 #triplefeeding is a technique with three main purposes:

1️⃣Bring the baby back to the breast.
2️⃣Increase or preserve mommy’s milk supply.
3️⃣Keep baby fed.

⚠️It is very demanding and requires professional supervision and close follow-up to see results. The reason we set a time frame is to make the process efficient and prevent those overlapping feedings.

🌈After two weeks of this mommy working hard on a triple feeding schedule, she was able to see an increase in her milk supply and a baby more willing to come to the breast. At our follow-up appointment, the baby was transferring more at the breast, and the milk supply increased. Now that the baby was in a better position to breastfeed, it was time to begin the process for a tongue-tie release.

🌟Triple feeding is an efficient technique that works in many cases, but it’s a TEMPORAL solution while we find out the root cause of the problem preventing that baby from nursing.

Triple feeding. This is a commonly recommended practice when exclusive breast/chest feeding is the goal, but for some reason isn’t able to happen right away. This may be due to latch or transfer issues, supply issues, or even anatomical issues with the lactating person or baby. 

It involves attempting to directly feed baby, working on latch or transfer as needed. After direct feeding, baby is then immediately bottle fed either expressed human milk or formula to ensure adequate intake. Finally, the lactating person is to express (usually with pumping) to stimulate further milk production. This whole cycle can take over an hour, and when baby is eating every 2-3 hours it leaves little to no time for anything else. 

Triple feeding isn’t bad, but it IS exhausting. It shouldn’t be recommended without a finite, measurable, short term goal. And if that goal isn’t met then a plan to stop needs to take its place. It is vital that the lactating person has adequate support while triple feeding: someone to ensure they are eating, someone who can bottle feed baby, and ensuring at least one 5 hour stretch of sleep in a 24 hour period. 

Let us know your experiences Triple Feeding - did it work? How long did you do it? What issues needed to be corrected to be able to exclusively breast/chest feed?

I say trigger warning because for some of us in this space, triple feeding brings back memories of guilt and feelings of inadequacy, anxiety, stress, and depression. 

I've done it, I've been there. And hope to NEVER have to do it again. 

I've also recommended it in lactation care plans, BUT not without a ton of other resources, explainantions, and referrals to other professionals and specialists.

So let's discuss, what is triple feeding and why is it recommended in breastfeeding care plans? 

❔WHAT---
The act of nursing, pumping, and supplementing all in the same feeding session. Typically first nurse the baby, then pump and simultaneously bottle feed if you have leftover milk or formula from a previous session, or pump first and bottle feed after.
THE GOOD: can help to increase supply, can help littles gain weight
THE BAD: super exhausting and time consuming
THE UGLY: often not something mother's chose, usually in response to low supply concerns, little not gaining which leads to ugly tears for everyone involved and sometimes a spin out into PPA and PPD; triple feeding can be too much of a mental overload and has been known to cause PTSD associated with breastfeeding thus causing many mamas to stop

❔WHY--
Well that's a loaded question so here's the scoop. When recommended as a part of lactation care appropriately, triple feeding is a SHORT term solution to a (hopefully) short term issue i.e. secondary low supply, little not transferring well, TOTs revision(s), weight gain concerns etc. However, some providers will suggest continuing triple feeding past a few weeks thus causing mamas to feel even more discouraged, stressed, guilty...all of the above. 

🩹Triple feeding is not a sustainable means to continue breastfeeding. That's why it is so important to find a provider that understands your goals as well as how to get to the root of why you are having breastfeeding issues...as opposed to just slapping the triple feeding band-aid. 

Has triple feeding ever been recommended for you and your little? Do you feel it was done appropriately? Share you experience below if you are comfortable. 

As always, I'm here for support if needed. ♥️

TRIPLE FEEDING

Let’s get this out of the way, Triple Feeding is a band aid. It is NOT meant as a long-term solution. 

So what’s the point?

The purpose is to assess overall milk supply and assess baby’s ability to remove milk. Triple feeding can be used to increase milk supply (if necessary), promote weight gain, and boost energy to nurse. 

Depending on the goal, the steps can be switched up a bit. So triple feeding can look like…

Nurse -> Pump -> Supplement  OR  Nurse -> Supplement -> Pump

Sounds great, but what’s the catch?

Triple feeding is EXHAUSTING! Imagine nursing for 30 minutes, pumping for 30 minutes, feeding pumped milk/donor milk/formula via bottle or SNS for 30 minutes… then… cleaning all pumping parts and bottles while baby sleeps. And repeating at least every 3 hours. 

This isn’t sustainable long term. Don’t get me wrong, triple feeding can be a great tool. But, there needs to be a plan to move past triple feeding. 

Work with your pediatrician and a lactation professional to ensure you have as much support as possible!

If you’re concerned about your baby’s intake, your supply, or baby’s weight, reach out! I’m here to help!

Yes, to a point we need to turn the suction up on our pumps to get milk out, but it should never hurt and all pumpers respond to the pump differently.  Here are some things to think about when it comes to pump suction:

💧If your suction is up so high that it is hurting, it will hurt your milk supply.  Pain blocks the hormone oxytocin which releases milk so if it hurts.  Therefore, if it hurts it's hurting milk removal (also if it's hurting, get a flange fitting consult!!)

💧Some pumpers respond better to lower suction and higher speed, some respond better to higher suction lower speed.  Everyone is different.

💧Many pumpers find that after a certain level of pump suction, they don't get more out if they crank it up higher.

💧Sometimes a higher suction means the milk will come quicker, but you will not actually get more milk.

💧Sometimes cranking the suction up to the highest level can cause damage to your nipples.  Be gentle to yourself!

💧If you feel like your pump is not removing milk as it should, instead of cranking it up, see an IBCLC. It could be the pump, it could be the flange, it could be a breast issue.

Listened to a webinar from United States Lactation Consultant Association this weekend while prepping my upcoming CLE training, and came across this little gem. The concept is to add a pump while baby is breastfeeding, in the early days to help get baby maximum milk intake.
Because breasts work in tandem with their letdowns (great for twins when you are tandem feeding) you can both capture a let down on the pump side, and also encourage let down on the baby's side. Double win right there.
The extra milk can be used to supplement a sleepy or jaundiced new baby after the feed, saved for the next feeding if a supplement is needed, or stored for later use. 
Many families ask me when they can start pumping, and especially those who are going back to work as they are feeling the pressure to start collecting milk. If breastfeeding is going well, you can start pumping anytime. If it is not going well, you will likely need to start pumping right away. So it pays to have a pump that you can easily use that works well for you.
I just loved this concept because it doesn't interfere with breastfeeding, but it gives parents that option of capturing lost milk that leaks on the other side, utilizes both breasts at each feeding (even if baby will only take one) and it has numerous applications for babies who need supplements, such as triple feeding which can be so exhausting and overwhelming for everyone in the family.
For this approach you can use any electric pump, a hand pump, or even a silicone pump like a Haakaa. 
Have you tried it? What was your experience?

Is your newborn super sleepy? Does he fall asleep all the time during feeding? Does he go from totally asleep to crying with no in between? Does he scream when the breast is offered and will only take a bottle?

Babies need to be in a certain “state” to be successful with feeding, either with breast or bottle, and so many babies struggle with this in the first several weeks of life.

Much of this can have to do with labor and delivery, postnatal issues such as jaundice or respiratory struggles, but the impact on feeding goes on long after they are “healthy”. 

State regulation, or your baby’s ability to move through the 6 states (deep sleep, light sleep, drowsiness, quiet alert, active alert, crying), is totally intertwined with their ability to feed. 

Poor transfer at the breast can have more to do with state regulation than sucking skills.

Limited intake or prolonged feedings can too.

Inability to latch can be due to your baby’s inability to stay calm and organized.

There are so many reasons for early feeding difficulties and getting the right strategies in place as soon as possible is so important in order to meet your feeding goals.

If any of this sounds like your baby and what you are going through, reach out today to get your personalized, research-based feeding plan in place with an expert by your side.

Closing out September with some well written info on PCOS.

Reposted from @lowmilksupplyfoundation We couldn’t let September pass by without discussing Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), one of the leading causes of infertility and a commonly seen disorder among those with chronic low milk supply. 

PCOS is thought to be the most common hormonal disorder among women of childbearing age, affecting as many as 1 in 4 women between the ages of 18 and 44. As a “syndrome,” PCOS can vary in the way it presents; symptoms can also change over time. It is also incredibly underdiagnosed.

PCOS is fundamentally a women’s health issue that can have profound long-term mental and physical health impacts. And it is unacceptable that a condition that affects so many women is so little understood. We must join together to demand better from our healthcare providers, and our healthcare system in general -- better understanding, better research, better support and better treatments!

This picture is the beginning of the hardest thing I’ve ever had to do.

Our journey started out in the hospital, where I was told I had to feed her every 2 hours to help get her bili levels down. We would literally scrape the colostrum out of the pumping equipment just to fill a syringe so we could tube feed her after she would try to breastfeed.

Then it turned to many sleepless nights because she’d wake up almost every hour to eat. Finally, we realized she was just wanting to cuddle with momma rather than eat.

That led to triple feedings, exclusive pumping, back to triple feedings, then eventually it led to whatever she wanted to do & felt comfortable with. If she wants mommy & wants to breastfeed, we do. If she wants a bottle, we make a bottle.

My life now centers around when she needs to eat & when I can pump. It’s hard. It’s tiring. It makes life so much more complicated than it use to be.

At the same time, it’s amazing to be able to give my baby the nourishments she needs to survive. I’m grateful to be able to have those special moments with her, and to have been able to be on this journey with her for almost 5 months now.

I’m so thankful for my mom, aunts, and cousins who’ve helped me so much along the way. I’m thankful for friends who don’t mind me pumping before we go places. I’m thankful for coworkers who step up so I can pump in between procedures. I’m thankful for my husband who learned all the things we needed to know about pumping & didn’t care if I pumped or breastfed.

For all the mamas out there struggling through this journey, too, no matter how long your journey was, I applaud you! For all the mamas out there who decided this journey wasn’t for you, I applaud you too, because let’s be honest, fed is best!

Disclaimer: This is my personal experience breastfeeding my baby. Please dont comment that breast is best. We all know how amazing breastmilk is & yes breastmilk should be a parents first choice. BUT FED IS BEST! 

Ever since I could remember I wanted to breastfeed my baby. I had dreams when I was pregnant of breastfeeding my baby. I did all the research, read all the books, watched all videos and we still had a ROUGH experience. To begin, when he was born, I had a rough afterbirth which led to a postpartum hemorrhage and a retained placenta. Looking back, this delayed alot of things regarding milk production for me. Considering the release of your placenta signals your body to make prolactin(your milk making hormone) 🤷🏻‍♀️ Anyways, he latched right away after I recovered from that. 40 min after he was born was when I first started feeding him. We fed every 2 hrs after that. I thought he was getting something and in hindsight he wasnt getting enough(even though babies have small stomachs that young, yes I know. He still wasnt getting enough) Anyways, We had latch issues the whole time in the hospital. The day we left I asked for formula because I had a feeling he wasnt drinking enough. He gulped the formula down so fast.... I felt soo terrible. My baby was hungry 😥 Regardless, I made sure he was always fed appropriately after that. He was admitted the next day back to the hospital for jaundice which is probably related to him not getting enough the first two days. 

I have to skip over the part of him being admitted back into the hospital for jaundice because thats another story. 

I have seen so many LC and only one told me he had a tongue and lip tie. So we went and got them both clipped. Poor baby still couldn’t latch properly to get milk even after that. Maybe 1 oz after 30 min. He took 3oz a feed at this time so 1 oz doesnt cut it. I triple fed for a week till I couldnt do it anymore. If you know what triple feeding is you’d understand.  So I went to exclusively pumping.... EP ISNT FOR THE WEAK(it is not the easy way, its the hard way) I pumped 8x a day for 8 weeks.

Posted @withregram • @kellyibclc Breastfeeding Bandaids can be needed, but should always be a short term solution while the root cause of the issue is figured out.⁠ Bandaids can help symptoms but not solve problems. 
⁠
🔶NIPPLE SHIELDS:⁠
Nipple shields are often used when a baby can't latch or when there is pain with latching.  Neither situation is normal and the cause should be figured out in order to make a plan to get off the nipple shield.⁠
⁠
🔶PUMPING AFTER BREASTFEEDS⁠
Sometimes parents pump after feeds at the breast in order to increase supply so the baby has more easy milk.  Again, this can be effective short term, but the baby should be able to maintain milk supply on his own and often there are simple solutions to help baby do this and decrease that workload for mama.⁠
⁠
🔶TRIPLE FEEDING⁠
Triple feeding is when you feed at the breast, pump and then feed that milk back either via bottle, finger feeding, cup feeding etc.  Triple feeding, like other bandaids, can be needed short term.  However, it is too much work to be a long term solution. ⁠
⁠
🔶REFLUX MEDS⁠
True acid reflux in babies is rare and usually only seen in preterm babies.  More commonly I see reflux due to swallowing air either because of a bad latch or because of an uncoordinated swallow OR reflux due to a food sensitivity.  Either way reflux meds are a bandaid to cover up why it is happening and this bandaid is not benign.  These meds were never studied on babies for safety, but retrospective research has shown that when given as a baby, they increase the baby's chances of broken bones as a child.⁠
⁠
🔶NIPPLE CREAM⁠
There are some great and not so great nipple creams out there for damaged nipples, but either way, they shouldn't be relied upon long term to keep pain or damage at bay. 
⁠
If you are using a bandaid and want to stop, find someone that is willing to dig in the weeds with you and figure out the root cause and also a way to fix that root cause!⁠
⁠

It's been awhile since I posted properly.  Life has been... Hectic? Since the children went back to school!!! But, I'm hoping to get back into the groove, and thought I would start with a little bit about silicone suction pumps! 

They really ARE pumps. 

They can stimulate your supply and in some people can lead to issues with oversupply if you are not careful.  I'm not saying don't use one, far from it, they are a great tool that has its time and place.  I used mine whilst triple feeding littlest miss if I didn't have time to get the double electric out, or for when out and about / nighttime expressing it was great.  But please use them with support, and learn a little about them first.  If you are prone to blocked ducts/mastitis/oversupply please speak to a infant feeding Supporter before hand.

It's also handy to remember, that just like ANY form of expressing, a silicone pump might not work for you!  Some breasts just do not react to a pump like they do a child, and for some people that can be completely normal!

Triple feeding is a very common recommendation that is made to many parents in the early days of feeding your infant. 

Perhaps baby isn't latching well or weight gain isn't what we expect.

Nursing your baby then pumping and topping up with that pumped milk and/ or formula encourage your supply to increase and your baby to gain weight. 

But its EXHAUSTING

When a client tells me that they have been triple feeding for any amount of time I ask how they are doing with it and then talk about options. 

A feeding tube at the breast, or SNS, can be used to cut down on the time triple feeding takes and to get baby feeling full while nursing. They receive the supplement and your breastmilk at the same time all while stimulating supply.

Durning pregnancy, and even before pregnancy, I never even considered how much of a challenge breastfeeding can be. I have caught myself in multiple acts of jealousy in these last five weeks post birth. Jealous of the moms that can just "whip out the boob" and feed their baby. My breastfeeding journey with my daughter has been an ongoing struggle. I struggle with producing enough milk for Magnolia. It's something I have to put .uch effort in to. She also has a tongue tie and a very weak latch, making it difficult for her to transfer the milk from my breast to her mouth. She was losing weight and we were having a hard time getting her back to her birth weight in the first couple weeks. 

After seeing lactation consultant, whom we now have been seeing almost weekly, we came up with the plan to do triple feeds. Althouhh its been successful in helping her gain weight, putting her to the breast, then offering her a bottle, then pumping is extremely time consuming and not to mention exhausting & overwhelming. It's a daunting task when you think about it. My nipples were bleeding, scabbing and ever so sore but I decided to keep pushing on because I want my baby to consume my breastmilk for as long as my body is willing to produce it. 

My mind keeps asking, is this worth it? I answer yes & no. Yes, because my daughter is getting food that my amazing body is making just for her. That in itself is incredible. No, because all this time I spend worrying about my breasts and extracting milk from them, I could be spending that time snuggling with my baby girl. It's honestly a mindfuck.

We just have to remember that our worth is not measured by how many ounces we produce or how our babies are fed. I salute any mama out there that is feeding their babies. Whether its formula, exclusively breastfeeding, exclusively pumping, triple feeding or any other method- you all are rockstars. Our babies will love us no differently at the end of the day.
