It is common for women in the early days to find themselves triple feeding their newborn. 
Triple feeding is when baby breastfeeds, mum expresses milk after and then supplements the baby that expressed breastmilk via syringe or bottle.  Or in some instances formula may be used if mum's supply is still coming in.

This can be daunting for new families.

The idea is that 'stimulating' the breast intensely will encourage more milk and therefore boost baby's weight gains or flush jaundice levels out or help a newborn that cannot successfully get everything they need at the breast.

Having to do this requires much effort, is physically exhausting and prolongs feeding times. 

It is not a long term solution. 

If you are discharged from hospital with this type of plan, seek help quickly from an IBCLC to assess your situation.  An IBCLC will be able to offer alternatives, assess your feeding technique and offer solutions for you.

Being a new mom is tough. When you are trying to breastfeed for the first time, it’s even tougher. I remember how difficult it was for me to wrap my head around all my issues breastfeeding. As a new mom, I encountered low milk supply due to milk transfer issues, tongue tie, supplementing, triple feeding, exclusively pumping every 2 hours, several IBCLC appointments, chiropractor, OT and two tongue tie revision surgeries. The problems seemed endless as if we don’t have enough to deal with as a new mom! You can definitely have emotional turmoil. As we get close to Mother’s Day here’s how you can really support the new mom in your life in those first couple of months postpartum:
.
- Listen to her, but don’t try to fix all her issues. Sometimes (most of the time) we just want to be heard, we want to vent without judgement as we share our emotions and struggles. .
.
- Make her life easier. This could mean cooking her a meal, helping her clean, sending her a care package, changing a diaper.
.
- Encourage her and tell her that she is resilient! You have no idea how a few words can empower someone who is so vulnerable. .
.
- If you see her be inpatient, angry or sad…let her be, for a moment. At times we need to exhibit our emotions as they come, raw and pure without fear of being criticized. Being a new mom is hard, remember that. .
.
- Help her discover her mama instinct! This is so important. As new moms we question our decision making so often, but there is something inside us all that helps us guide this new life we just birthed. Help her realize that her gut instinct means the best for her baby, and she should listen to it.
.
- Support her. Just be there. Hold her hand as she slowly and naturally becomes a Mother. Love her through this transition and watch her transform, you’ll be amazed. .

As an #ibclc I see many many mothers who triple feed their babies.
Triple feeding, in case you don't know:
- direct breastfeeding as much as possible
- pumping breastmilk
- supplementing with formula or expressed milk 
all alongside each other. 

A REAL KILLER! Totally unsustainable for long periods of time. Hands up in the comments if you have triple fed and tell us how long. 
How did it/ does it feel? Does it feel like you have zero time to look after your own needs? Like you are drowning in washing and sterilising bottles, pumping and feeding and actually have no time to enjoy your baby? Like this is NOT what you signed up for?

I see you! You're not alone. 
I have worked with family after family where this type of feeding was getting the better of them and they cried out for help!

The confusion is real. How much milk do you give as a supplement? How long do you pump for? Do you have to sterilise after each feed? How long between weighing sessions? Is it safe to reduce top ups or are you risking baby's health? Is it OK to let baby sleep for longer periods of time? And the questions just go on and on...

Every case is so very unique and individual. 

I will need to check baby's general health history, alongside the mother's. 
I will need to get some idea of baby's feeding patterns and efficiency at the breast/bottle.
I will need to watch your breastfeeding and bottle feeding technique. 
I will ask you how much you pump and how much formula you use daily. 
We will check your pump flange fit.
Your lifestyle, diet and mental health, medication etc etc.

Don't suffer alone.

Why I don’t recommend triple feeding.

Ultimately for most Moms it will end in burn out and studies show Moms who triple feed end breastfeeding early. 

Triple feeding can be a useful SHORT TERM tool if Mom has a lot of support at home. Most Moms who triple feed spend on average 45 minutes to 1 hour to complete the triple feed cycle. Can you imagine spending 8-12 hours a day on feeding!

 It’s a bandaid. Instead we should focus on the root cause of why Mom needs to triple feed. 

✨bad latch
✨Tension
✨Tongue tie
✨Perceived low supply

Always ask questions, get help, there are solutions!

"Triple feeding"....what is that?

Work and exhaustion, that's what it is.  Moms who have done it know the deal.

Triple feeding refers to a routine involving breastfeeding, pumping, then bottle feeding a baby.

It's recommended when there is an issue with milk supply or baby's weight gain/intake.

It should NEVER be a long term solution. 

It's labor, requires support around the mother, because her entire life will revolve around feeding.  Feeding newborns is intense when things are going well....add two steps to the routine, and the time it takes to feed exponentially increases.

It's effective....but there are a lot of ways to stabilize a breastfeeding situation.  If triple feeding is impossible for a family, there are other options. 

Seek skilled support by a lactation professional if you're having issues with supply or weight gain and have been advised to triple feed.  You should be given a plan to eventually STOP triple feeding.

Hey Pumpers!! Want to save some time?  You don't have to warm up the bottle every time you give breastmilk!  It is just as good for them when it's cold. ⁠
⁠
If your baby is use to it being warmed up and rejects the cold, you may have to do a gradual change. ⁠
⁠
If the milk has been in the refrigerator for a few days, it may need to be heated just enough to mix in the fats.⁠
⁠
ADDED BONUS - If you are also feeding at the breast, having the bottle milk cold, makes the milk straight from the source that much more appealing, leading to less bottle preference. ⁠
⁠
If you are an exclusive pumper, I suggest getting them use to a range of temperatures, so when you need to (like when you are out and about) you can serve cold milk, but when your home and want more comfort out of the milk, you can serve it warm. ⁠
⁠
Times when it's a good idea to warm it up. ⁠
- Sleep time - they will go to sleep easier with warm milk⁠
- If they are sick - just like you, warm liquids when sick feel better.⁠

Thankfully awareness of non-IgE allergies is becoming more common-which means more parents are getting the support they need to manage them. This type of allergy can be hard to diagnose and manage especially in little bubs.

Unfortunately, we do have the highest rates of food allergy in Australia with 1 in 10 infants having a food allergy. 

The really tricky thing is that a lot of the symptoms we see in non-IgE allergy are also similar to “normal newborn fusiness” and the spectrum of what is “normal” for baby poo can also make it confusing for parents. 

I have lost count of the number of parents I have seen that were told that their baby was just “purple crying” and that it was usual behaviour to be crying all day and night. That as long as they are gaining weight gain “it’s okay”…..Yes- some babies are more unsettled as they find their way in the world (it is a lot to get use to!) but if you also see this alongside other symptoms we have flagged I would really suggest you look into support to explore food allergy or intolerance. 

Lastly- even if it isn’t an underlying medical condition causing your little one to be more unhappy this doesn’t mean you don’t need or deserve support. Babies need us deeply and some babies need a lot more support than others. This in turn means we need to be supporting these parents more. So no matter the “why” behind “why” you’re having a hard time- ask for help and support. Find a GP that listens and gets to know your family. See your Maternal Child Health Nurse and ask what supports are available. Talk to a lactation consultant if breastfeeding isn’t feeling right. Chat to a dietitian if you think food is an issue before you start cutting anything out.

Nope, it doesn’t mean going back for third helpings of tiramisu. (Though I highly recommend doing so, if you have tiramisu around...)

It *does* mean this, usually in this order:

1. Feeding your baby at the breast
2. “Feeding” your pump by expressing breastmilk with a breast pump or hand expression 
3. Feeding your baby the aforementioned expressed milk — usually via bottle

Triple feeding is often recommended to parents of babies with possible oral restrictions (tongue, lip, cheek ties) as a way to help make sure baby is getting fed. 

For us, it was an excruciating process and nearly broke me. The entire process took about 1.5 hours from start to finish (20 min painful breastfeeding, 30 min pumping, 20 min bottle feeding with diaper changes throughout) — and by then it was nearly time to start all over again with our hungry newborn. 

We saw a stellar IBCLC (heyyy @ashleybenzibclc) who recommended SNS feeding to help cut our feeding time in half. This meant we used a tube to feed our gal expressed milk AT the breast and THEN pumped for the next feed. The time saved was a lifesaver — I was finally able to sleep for more than 20 minutes! 

There’s a lot of controversy over whether triple feeding is necessary for babies with ties. I can’t speak to that — but I can say it was the hardest thing I’ve ever done. We triple fed for nearly two months. I wouldn’t have made it through without support from an IBCLC, my fella, and our doula @theandrewaugust. Support is VITAL.

What you need to know about triple feeding:
Triple feeding involves feeding your baby at the breast,  topping the baby up with expressed milk or formula,  then pumping. What is a flange!? A flange, AKA a breast shield, is a key component to a breast pump. It is the part that fits directly over the nipple and areola. When the pump is activated, the flange helps to create a vacuum seal that mimics the baby’s sucking motion, facilitating the extraction of milk. Flanges come in many sizes to fit different nipple sizes and shapes, ensuring comfort and effective milk expression. Many pumps come with a standard size of 24 mm but guess what!! That is not the size most women will use. Average flange size is in the range of 13 mm to 19 mm! Using the wrong flange size can cause pain and inefficient milk collection. Proper fit is essential to prevent discomfort and maximize that milk output! To find more information on flange fit guidelines, check out https://www.babiesincommon.com/flange-fits-guide

Paced bottle feeding is a technique designed to mimic the natural rhythm of breastfeeding. It involves feeding the baby in a more controlled and slower manner, allowing them to drink at their own pace, similar to how they would nurse at the breast. This method helps prevent overfeeding and encourages the baby to self-regulate their milk intake.

👶🏼Positioning: The baby is held in an upright position rather than lying flat. This helps them control the flow of milk more effectively.
 🍼Bottle Angle: The bottle is held horizontally, which slows down the flow of milk. The nipple is filled only halfway with milk, so the baby has to actively suck to draw out the milk.
🐌Pauses: Regular breaks are taken during the feeding to allow the baby to catch their breath, swallow, and decide if they want more milk. This mimics the natural pauses that occur during breastfeeding.

Why should you Pace Bottle feed:
1. Prevents Overfeeding: Babies have small stomachs and can easily be overfed if the milk flow is too fast. Paced feeding allows them to eat until they are satisfied, reducing the risk of overeating and discomfort.
2. Supports Breastfeeding: For breastfed babies who also take bottles, this method helps them transition more easily between breast and bottle. It maintains a feeding pace similar to breastfeeding.
3. Reduces Gas and Reflux: The slower feeding pace can minimize the amount of air a baby swallows, reducing the risk of gas, spit-up, and reflux.

💛Paced bottle feeding is a beneficial approach for all babies, whether they are exclusively bottle-fed, combination fed, or transitioning between different feeding methods. It supports their physical and emotional well-being by allowing them to eat at a pace that suits their individual needs.

Triple feeding can be an effective way to help preserve breast milk supply if there are any transfer issues such as lip tie, tongue tie, or latch difficulties. It may be preferable to first nurse then pump and use that pumped milk to bottle feed baby. If baby isn't one to wait after nursing for you to pump then you can switch up the order.

We also use triple feeding as a tool to try and up milk supply. People may see an increase after trialing for a week or so. I prefer to nurse, bottlefeed, then pump so that baby doesn't get impatient or to nurse then bottle feed while I pump to cut the time down.

Try to keep the time between the end of your nursing session to the start of your pumping session under 15 minutes; the body will then register it as one milk removal and as a signal to hopefully produce more from that feed. If longer it will register more like an additional removal- which can also have its benefits- but isn't as closely aligned with the triple feeding goal.

Triple feeding is temporary. We are either using it as a protective measure until we are able to transfer milk effectively while nursing or are trying to up supply. If using it to up production and you see an increase then you have your increase; baby can remove the additional milk and you can stop. If you see no increase then there's no need to continue. While triple feeding can be useful, breastfeeding should be sustainable. Triple feeding is an option- not a necessity- even with low supply or transfer difficulties. You know what works best for you and baby.

Sometimes parents find themselves triple feeding – feeding baby at the breast, offering a top-up of either expressed milk or formula and then pumping. If you have ever done this, then hats off to you; it’s ridiculously hard work!

Triple feeding can be suggested when a baby hasn’t gained sufficient weight. The idea is sound – you feed baby at the breast but then give them a little extra to boost their weight gain while pumping to increase or maintain your milk supply.
 
But the reality can be very challenging. We know that breastfed babies feed very regularly in the early weeks and so parents can find that by the time they’ve completed all three steps, it’s time to start over again. This can very quickly become overwhelming!

The good news is that triple feeding is meant to be a temporary strategy, and it is usually entirely possible to get to the point where top-ups and pumping sessions are slowly decreased to the point where they are no longer needed. 

There are some tips that can help while triple feeding:
• Getting someone else to give the top-up can mean that you can get on with pumping immediately after the feed at the breast. 
• If this isn’t possible then a hands-free pumping bra can allow you to feed baby their top-up while you pump. 
• Giving the top up at the breast using an at-breast supplementer may also be an option to combine two of the jobs
• Sometimes you may end up missing a pumping session – this is ok. Occasionally something has to give, and a little break can be the thing that keeps you going for the next day or two. 

However, my biggest tip, if you find yourself triple feeding is to seek out some specialist breastfeeding support. Slow weight gain is often due to ineffective milk transfer at the breast and so getting an IBCLC to do a full feeding assessment and support you to make changes is wise. If an ineffective latch isn’t the cause of the insufficient weight gain, then an IBCLC would be able to explore other possible causes with you and work alongside you to create a plan for going forward.

Thankfully awareness of non-IgE allergies is becoming more common-which means more parents are getting the support they need to manage them. This type of allergy can be hard to diagnose and manage especially in little bubs.

Unfortunately, we do have the highest rates of food allergy in Australia with 1 in 10 infants having a food allergy.

The really tricky thing is that a lot of the symptoms we see in non-IgE allergy are also similar to “normal newborn fusiness” and the spectrum of what is “normal” for baby poo can also make it confusing for parents.

I have lost count of the number of parents I have seen that were told that their baby was just “purple crying” and that it was usual behaviour to be crying all day and night. That as long as they are gaining weight gain “it’s okay”…..Yes- some babies are more unsettled as they find their way in the world (it is a lot to get use to!) but if you also see this alongside other symptoms we have flagged I would really suggest you look into support to explore food allergy or intolerance.

Lastly- even if it isn’t an underlying medical condition causing your little one to be more unhappy this doesn’t mean you don’t need or deserve support. Babies need us deeply and some babies need a lot more support than others. This in turn means we need to be supporting these parents more. So no matter the “why” behind “why” you’re having a hard time- ask for help and support. Find a GP that listens and gets to know your family. See your Maternal Child Health Nurse and ask what supports are available. Talk to a lactation consultant if breastfeeding isn’t feeling right. Chat to a dietitian if you think food is an issue before you start cutting anything out.

*not all symptoms here will be present or in the same degree. This is not an exclusive list.

This position for paced bottle feeding is great for babies under 3 months old.  Paced bottle feeding is important for those going back and forth between breast and bottle.  However, I find that sitting them upright doesn't work well for all babies, especially tinies because they don't have enough support for their bodies.  I find that sometimes when parents or caregivers are trying to sit up newborns to pace bottle feed, the newborn collapses in and then isn't in a good position to feed.  This solves that problem. 

Reasons to Pace Bottle Feed:
💧You can keep a baby from eating too quickly and overfeeding
💧Baby is able to regulate their suck, swallow, breath pattern without milk dripping in their mouth
💧Baby can regulate their own feed
💧You can pace the feed similar to the pace at the breast
💧Baby will not prefer bottle flow to the breast flow - especially when milk supply isn't huge.  Humans will always choose the path of least resistance and if it's way easier to drink from a bottle, they will choose it even if, in the end, easier does not mean better for them.

Other things to think about when pacing the feed.
🍼Hold the bottle horizontal
🍼Make sure their chin is not tucked down toward their chest
🍼If they are going back and forth between breast and bottle, don't give them milk right away.  Make them work for it.  Tip the bottle down a bit, so there is no milk in the nipple. They should suck suck suck for at least 10 seconds before they are rewarded with milk.  When at the breast, it typically takes at least that long to elicit a let down.  This makes it so they do not expect milk right away at breast and keeps frustrations at bay. 
🍼Take breaks throughout the feed by tipping the bottle slightly down.

“If you’re seeing a newborn with excessive weight loss in the first week, one of the first things to check is whether the birthing parent had IV fluids during labour and delivery.

This extra fluid can pass through the placenta to the baby, leading to an artificially elevated birth weight.

This is harmless to the newborn, as they will naturally just wee it out over the next day or so, but it can cause the appearance of excess weight loss in the newborn when they’re weighed a few days later.

The subsequent concerns about inadequate milk intake usually result in the recommendation to give supplemental feeds +/- pump to increase supply. Hello, triple feeding. Hello, top-up trap!

In this situation, using the weight at 24 hours (after the diuresis has occurred but before any true weight loss will have happened) as the “birth weight” can give a better representation of how feeding is going (along with the usual markers of output eg wees and poos)”

Breastfeeding isn't all or nothing.⁠

#breastfeeding isn't all or nothing. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months is the global guideline but if your journey looks a bit different you can be confident that the effort of providing any breastmilk to your baby is worth it. ⁠
⁠
Because of the way birth and the postnatal period is managed in our modern world,  breastfeeding initiation is sometimes not well-supported by the health care system (public and private) and formula top-ups are prescribed.  This might be temporary or an ongoing part of feeding a baby and can range from once a day to every feed.  Formula can even become the primary food source for many babies. However introducing formula doesn't have to mean ending breastfeeding.  If your baby is still going to the breast,  you can continue to offer it. The immune support and bonding continues to be important even if nutrition is not fully met at the breast. ⁠
⁠
If you are on the #triplefeeding cycle of feeding at the breast,  topping up with formula and/or expressed breastmilk or donor milk, followed by a session with the breast pump then you are practising the hardest method of feeding your baby. Something has to give but it doesn't have to be a total switch. You might choose to put your baby to the breast at alternate feeds and pump every second feed. You might decide to stop offering the breast and just pump. Or stop pumping and just offer the breast. You can choose to finish at the breast after every formula feed and enjoy your baby drifting off to sleep at your breast. You might find pumping is your preference to direct feeding or perhaps you hate the pump but enjoy direct feeding your baby, even if they are not effectively removing a full feed. ⁠
⁠
Breastfeeding can look very different and still be important to your baby. Using a supplementary nursing system (supply line) at some or all feed times.  Topping up with a small cup of your own expressed milk, #donormilk or formula after some or all feeds. There is no one right way and lots of flexibility. You can stop breastfeeding completely and then #relactate if you change your mind days or weeks later.

Sometimes parents find themselves triple feeding – feeding baby at the breast, offering a top-up of either expressed milk or formula and then pumping. If you have ever done this, then hats off to you; it’s ridiculously hard work!

Triple feeding can be suggested when a baby hasn’t gained sufficient weight. The idea is sound – you feed baby at the breast but then give them a little extra to boost their weight gain while pumping to increase or maintain your milk supply.
 
But the reality can be very challenging. We know that breastfed babies feed very regularly in the early weeks and so parents can find that by the time they’ve completed all three steps, it’s time to start over again. This can very quickly become overwhelming!

The good news is that triple feeding is meant to be a temporary strategy, and it is usually entirely possible to get to the point where top-ups and pumping sessions are slowly decreased to the point where they are no longer needed. 

There are some tips that can help while triple feeding:
• Getting someone else to give the top-up can mean that you can get on with pumping immediately after the feed at the breast. 
• If this isn’t possible then a hands-free pumping bra can allow you to feed baby their top-up while you pump. 
• Having extra pump parts can also mean that you don’t have to wash them after every pumping session. 
• Sometimes you may end up missing a pumping session – this is ok. Occasionally something has to give, and a little break can be the thing that keeps you going for the next day or two. 

However, my biggest tip, if you find yourself triple feeding is to seek out some specialist breastfeeding support. Slow weight gain is often due to ineffective milk transfer at the breast and so getting an IBCLC to do a full feeding assessment and support you to make changes is wise. If an ineffective latch isn’t the cause of the insufficient weight gain, then an IBCLC would be able to explore other possible causes with you and work alongside you to create a plan for going forward.

When a flange fits well, you should:

1. Feel comfortable for the total 15-20 minute pumping session
2. Get optimal milk output
3. Have no skin damage or blanching from pumping
4. See only the nipple moving in the flange tunnel, no areola

Just like when runners buy a new pair of running shoes, it’s a more involved process than simply measuring the length of the foot. You would try it on, see if it works with your favorite socks, make sure your heel doesn’t slip, make sure your toes don’t get blisters, etc.

Flange fitting is the same! It’s more than just measuring!

I remember my first born... things were going well in the hospital. Lactation nurse said all looked good. I felt confident; I mean breastfeeding is natural right? The baby should know exactly what to do! WRONG! I kept nursing and she was crying never content. My nipples were cracked and bleeding. Even a towel or my shirt/bra touching them hurt. So I booked an appointment with a lactation consultant. 
She said I had a low milk supply. I needed to nurse, supplement 1 to 2 oz of formula or pumped milk and then pump 8 to 10 times a day. Nights were the hardest. I skipped some pumping sessions and found out that this is the most critical time to pump. Hormones are highest and set tone for the day at night. Once I was disciplined about night pumping I got my supply up. But it was so hard. I was determined though. I also got an extension to my leave, had a supportive moms nursing group and supportive partner. I may have given up if it were different. Not all moms have these things. Moms need more support to be able to overcome these challenges. Breastfeeding is a learned skill but so worth it for the benefite to mom and baby.

We have been helping our mommy pump milk for our new, human baby brother. She spent 7.5 weeks #triplefeeding (breast feed + bottle feed + pumping every time the baby eats) using a hospital grade breast pump rented from #nursingmotherscouncel to get milk supply up to meet baby’s needs and because he had significant weight loss at 3 days of life. All of this combined with the support of some amazing PAMF lactation consultants, and now she is able to feed baby with breast milk from the boob, bottle, or #supplementalnursingsystem (SNS). They also helped with a feeding plan that supported breastfeeding from the beginning, so Mom was able to transition back from mostly bottle-feedings to mostly breastfeedings. We still help her pump 3 times a day to keep up with his nutrition needs and be able to have milk to supplement with.
We tend to think breastfeeding will just happen and feel like a failure as moms if it doesn’t, but many moms do have feeding challenges in some form. 
There are so many socioeconomic barriers to breastfeeding and our family has been so lucky! We live in California and have language in mom’s work contract that protects leave time and keep healthcare benefits so that mom and baby can take the time and access weekly lactation appointments and this crazy feeding schedule. We also live in an area with more access to lactation consultants through insurance or community, and access education and support through #nursingmotherscouncel and costly equipment and lactation paraphernalia through PAMF lactation and insurance.
There’s not anything wrong with formula-feeding or people who choose formula for one reason or another (and being able to supplement with formula when needed saved our family!), but we need to do more as a society to support breastfeeding and access for all than we are currently doing.
We are loving our new baby brother and all of his smells, and still take ever opportunity for mama snuggles that we can get.

Sometimes breastfeeding doesn't go as expected. If that's the case,  triple feeding may be able to help!

Even when things don't go as planned (really, does that ever happen?), it's still possible to work towards your goals. Remember to be flexible as needs change and challenges arise. Give yourself and your littles grace as you work through overcoming these challenges. 

One way to work through challenges is with triple feeding. Combining direct nursing, supplementing (either with pumped breastmilk or formula), and pumping is one method to overcome certain challenges. 

Be sure to work closely with your pediatrician, especially if weight loss or lack of weight gain is a problem. Working with a lactation professional can also be invaluable as you develop a plan for you and baby.

Triple Feeding is meant to be a short-term method used to increase milk supply, and to ensure adequate nutrition and weight gain in the infant. 

Triple feeding is exhausting and usually not sustainable as a long-term option. 

During triple feeding, during each and every feeding session, baby will:
-engage in direct breastfeeding
-have additional supplementation (via expressed/donor milk or formula via bottle, cup or similar)

“Bring baby it breast for each feed and then when they are finished, offer some formula to top them off.”

Have you heard this before?

Many well-intentioned health care providers give this advice, particularly if the baby is slow to gain weight, is still working on learning how to latch, or “until milk comes in.” Although there are times when formula is medically indicated in babies, there is a key piece of information that many people do not include in their advice.

What can happen is that babies get some breastmilk from feeding directly, and then take formula when offered. This can lead to babies feeling more full than they otherwise would have, which can lead to less frequent feeding at the breast or a less vigorous suck at the next feed.

So when the next feed comes around, baby may not remove as much milk. Parents worry because it was a short feed and offer formula again, which the baby often takes. This cycle continues and the baby may feed less and less at the breast, which can ultimately lead to a decline in milk production, which further perpetuates less feeding at the breast and more from the bottle.

So what to do if your baby is not feeding effectively at the breast? Bring them to breast, pump, and then give the pumped milk. If there is not enough milk to give, THEN give formula when indicated. The key is to pump every time that formula is give, so that your body gets the stimulation it needs to keep making milk!

When breastfeeding isn’t working
It is so important to be honest about what to expect with breastfeeding in the early days. Whilst it's natures way of feeding our babies it doesn’t always come naturally. Some women may struggle with the following difficulties from birth:
- Non latching babies
- Significant pain and trauma to the nipples
- Delay in transition from colostrum to mature milk
- Low milk supply

I want to acknowledge these potential challenges, not to put you off breastfeeding, but to ensure that it doesn't derail your breastfeeding journey. Challenges can be overcome! Early & appropriate intervention is key to having the best likelihood of success.

If you encounter difficulties in the early days of breastfeeding there are 3 things you need to do-
1. Seek immediate, qualified breastfeeding SUPPORT.
It can be helpful pre-birth to identify where you are going to get help if you need it.

2. FEED your baby
If your baby can latch and if you are physically able to feed, then do this at the breast. If there are weight concerns, reduced nappy output or low milk supply you will likely also need to pump after feeds and top up.
If you can’t feed at the breast or if you need to top up,  this can be done via an alternative method such as syringe, finger feeding, cup feeding or bottle.

3. PUMP to tell the breasts they need to make milk.
If your baby is not latching or you can't latch them due to pain/trauma then pump a minimum of 8 times in 24 hours and feed that milk to your baby while healing/working on latching.

If you're breastfeeding but there are concerns that baby is not getting enough milk (weight/nappies best indicators)then continue to breastfeed, pump then top up with your milk. This is known as triple feeding. It is only a short term fix as part of a monitored feeding plan. You would do this a minimum of 8 times in 24 hours.
In the event there is a shortfall of milk then use formula alongside. As your breast milk increases through feeding and pumping, the formula top ups will be replaced with breast milk top ups.

We’ve just come to the end of a week of “triple feeding” (breastfeed - pump - bottle)  due to a poor latch because of a recently diagnosed submucosal or faux tongue tie leading to faltering weight gain - again!! 

That meant for each feed, we’ve been offering each breast twice (so 4 lots of boob!), swapping to the other side as soon as the rhythmic deep suck and swallows subside. Then after that, expressing with the pump to make sure each breast is empty, then offering that milk in a bottle! 🍼 All to help increase my supply, and get some weight on this kid!! 

Each cycle takes us about an hour to 90 minutes, with winding breaks and a mid feed nappy change. Baby has time for a nap 😴 while I sterilise the pump, grab a cuppa ☕️ and run for a wee! She’s been feeding about every 2 hours so we have about half hour before we start all over again! 🙈

To say I’ve been knackered is an understatement! 🤣 But… after only 4 days she had gained 140g which is her biggest ever gain in the shortest amount of time. 🙌 Totally worth it! My supply has been ‘reset’ and baby is feeding much more efficiently. 

We also went for a session of #craniosacraltherapy yesterday, and already baby’s tongue is looser and has a wider range of movement! The tightness in her jaw seems to be resolving and her mouth is now opening wider!! 😁 All this has lead to a much better, deeper latch this morning and better use of her tongue at the breast! 🙌

Moving forward, we’re continuing with the double 2 sided feeding and hoping and praying for a massive gain on the scales on Monday!! 🤞

I can’t believe we’ve been on this faltering weight gain journey since day 5 post birth - baby is 8 weeks old next week! 🤷‍♀️ It’s been tough, mentally and physically, but I really hope we’ve finally identified all the causes (with the silent reflux diagnosis a few weeks ago too) and baby’s weight will just keep going up!!
